This is a model of how bodies of understanding emerge—a pattern you see over and over in industry after industry. Let me describe it in the context of the organic chemical industry.
00:57
Eighty years ago, if you needed a new molecule, there were only about 50 people in the whole world who could synthesize these molecules. Dupont employed almost all of them. These people were deeply experienced—the best in the world.
When they needed to develop a new molecule, they would just reach deep and pull out all the intuition and education they could, try to synthesize something, mix a few atoms in a beaker, spin it into a fiber, and then knock on a colleague’s door: “What do you think? I just invented this.” The colleague would say, “I have no idea what you invented, but bring it in. Let’s heat it up for 10 more minutes and see what happens.”
The miracle molecules we now call nylon, polyester, acetate, Kevlar, and so on emerged from DuPont’s labs through this trial-and-error problem-solving process. Only the best in the world could play in this game.
01:44
As these artists practiced their craft over subsequent decades, patterns began to emerge. When organic chemistry moved from trial-and-error into pattern recognition, people could start teaching others how to build these molecules. There wasn’t a handbook yet, but there were patterns. You could tell your students, “If you do this, there’s a higher probability this will happen than that.”
You didn’t have to be the smartest in the world to play in this game. As a result, more people studied organic chemistry, more companies entered the fiber business, and eventually, theories like quantum theory and rate theory emerged.
03:15
As these theories, which are statements of causality, became understood, you could predict in advance that if you do this, this will be the result. You could build models to know whether a particular molecule could be built and what its properties would be. Today, if you need a new molecule, all you need is a BS in chemistry from a state school and a great piece of software. You can build better molecules faster and cheaper than the world’s best scientists of a few generations ago.
04:33
The progress from trial-and-error to pattern recognition to rules-based understanding has been a blessing to mankind. Before you go to bed at night, look around the room you’re sleeping in. You can touch at least a dozen different fibers that have been an unmitigated blessing in terms of quality, reliability, cost, performance, and durability.
These blessings didn’t come from replicating the intuition of DuPont scientists but from commoditizing their understanding through scientific progress.
05:21
The same thing is happening in medicine. Historically, and even today, if you have a problem, you go to the finest doctor you can find. They pull from their deepest experience and intuition and treat every patient as if they are different. Medicine has historically been intuitive.
As doctors practiced their craft, patterns emerged, leading to empirical or best-practices medicine. We’re not yet at rules-based medicine for many diseases, but the more we move from intuitive medicine to pattern recognition to rules-based precision medicine, the higher the quality and the lower the cost.
06:54
Venture capital, historically, has been in the realm of intuitive medicine. Many venture capitalists believe you can’t predict what will work or not, so they rely on their intuition for every potential investment. In my mind, entrepreneurship doesn’t need to be in the trial-and-error stage anymore. There is a lot that is now in the pattern recognition realm.
08:36
Some of my best friends are venture capitalists, but as a group, fewer have read my research than any other group. They believe the world is unpredictable and that they already know everything they need. I want to talk about components of patterns that increase the probability of success.
09:25
The most known piece of my work is the theory of disruption. I remember when Andy Grove gave a big talk at the Academy of Management. He organized his talk around disruption. It was lucky for me because I was coming up for tenure at Harvard. Grove told me, “You shouldn’t call it disruption; you should call it the Christensen effect.” Disruption has too many connotations, and people might misunderstand the theory. I couldn’t call it the Christensen effect, so I kept calling it disruption. Grove was right: everybody uses the word, but few understand it.
10:52
The theory of disruption allows you to predict competitive responses. It tells you whether your moves will kill incumbents or whether they will kill you. Companies, in pursuit of profit, continually improve products. If you try to win by introducing a better product for the best customers of an industry leader, they will always beat you.
12:16
Instead, if you enter at the bottom of a market with products that aren’t as good as the leader’s, but improve over time, the leader will flee upmarket rather than fight you. To kill the competitor rather than be killed, start at the bottom. All successful companies in Silicon Valley followed this pattern.
13:40
The second element relates to customers. If you have a new technology, don’t go after an established market. Compete against non-consumption.
14:27
Example: Electronics and the transistor. From the late 1940s to early 1970s, consumer electronics used vacuum tubes. They were expensive and large, so only wealthy people could afford TVs.
15:13
Transistors were a disruptive technology but couldn’t immediately replace vacuum tubes. Established companies tried to make them good enough for existing products, investing billions to overcome technical barriers.
16:47
In 1955, Sony released a $2 pocket radio. It was small, static-filled, and limited in quality, but infinitely better than nothing. Teenagers loved it because it let them listen to music privately. In 1959, Sony introduced the first portable television for $99. It was limited but accessible, delighting customers who had no other option. Over time, solid-state electronics improved, and vacuum tube companies vanished.
19:46
Lesson: Target customers whose alternative is nothing. Then, improve products iteratively.
20:26
Today, electric vehicles illustrate the same principle. Tesla’s $100k cars compete with the best vehicles in California. But the bigger opportunity is targeting parents of teenagers who need slow, short-range cars—infinitely better than nothing.
21:49
Similarly, solar electricity is not competitive in developed markets due to grid reliability. But in Mongolia, half the population has no electricity. Cheap solar products are infinitely better than nothing, creating a booming new market across Africa and Asia.
24:53
Lesson: With new technologies, compete against non-consumption first to increase your probability of success.
25:38
Third theory: Jobs to be Done. Understand what job the customer is trying to accomplish. People don’t buy based on characteristics; they hire products to get a job done.
26:27
Example: Milkshakes. A fast-food chain tried improving milkshakes using customer demographics—it didn’t work. Observation revealed morning commuters bought milkshakes for long, boring drives.
30:29
Alternatives like bananas, donuts, bagels, and Snickers didn’t work as well. Milkshakes satisfied the job: filling, long-lasting, easy to consume while driving. Competitors were other ways to accomplish the job, not other milkshakes.
32:24
The job, not the customer, is the correct unit of analysis. Designing products around the job dramatically increases success probability.
33:06
Finally, venture capital itself needs disruption. When I started my first company in 1984, Bain Capital invested in Staples. Later, as funds grew, they moved upmarket to bigger deals. Entrepreneurs at the low end struggle to get funding due to this mismatch.
36:49
That concludes my prepared remarks. Now, you can ask me questions about how venture capital and entrepreneurship might get disrupted.

---

🧠 **From Intuition to Architecture: Why Design Needs Its Own Scientific Revolution**  

In one of his Startup Grind talks, Clayton Christensen shared a timeless pattern he observed across industries — from chemistry to medicine to entrepreneurship.  

At first, every new field starts as *art*.  
A few gifted people use intuition, trial and error, and instinct to build something new.  

Then, over time, **patterns** begin to emerge.  
People recognize what works more often than not.  
Craft evolves into *practice*.  

Eventually, theory and systems take over — we learn *why* things work, not just *what* works.  
And when that happens, **knowledge scales**. You don’t need the world’s best chemist anymore to make nylon; you just need the right framework and software.  

That same evolution is happening — or *should* be happening — in **product design**.  

Right now, many teams still design by intuition.  
We make decisions based on taste, stakeholder preferences, or sprint pressure.  
But as patterns emerge — in research, flows, and feedback loops — we gain the opportunity to move design from *intuition* to *architecture*.  

Design systems are part of this shift, but they’re only the beginning.  
The real transformation happens when we start building **product architecture** — causal models that help us predict outcomes:  

- If we simplify this flow, activation increases.  
- If we remove this step, trust decreases.  
- If we shift this moment of friction, retention improves.  

That’s design turning into science — not decoration.  

As Christensen said:  
> “The progress from trial-and-error to pattern recognition to rules-based understanding has been a blessing to mankind.”  

We’re entering that same phase in design.  
The question is whether we’ll treat it like an art we guard — or a system we scale.  

🎥 Watch the full talk here:  
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RQSG_d0mmf0

In my mind, entrepreneurship doesn’t need to be in the trial-and-error stage anymore. There is a lot that is now in the pattern recognition realm.
08:36
Some of my best friends are venture capitalists, but as a group, fewer have read my research than any other group. They believe the world is unpredictable and that they already know everything they need. I want to talk about components of patterns that increase the probability of success.
09:25
The most known piece of my work is the theory of disruption. I remember when Andy Grove gave a big talk at the Academy of Management. He organized his talk around disruption. It was lucky for me because I was coming up for tenure at Harvard. Grove told me, “You shouldn’t call it disruption; you should call it the Christensen effect.” Disruption has too many connotations, and people might misunderstand the theory. I couldn’t call it the Christensen effect, so I kept calling it disruption. Grove was right: everybody uses the word, but few understand it.
10:52
The theory of disruption allows you to predict competitive responses. It tells you whether your moves will kill incumbents or whether they will kill you. Companies, in pursuit of profit, continually improve products. If you try to win by introducing a better product for the best customers of an industry leader, they will always beat you.
12:16
Instead, if you enter at the bottom of a market with products that aren’t as good as the leader’s, but improve over time, the leader will flee upmarket rather than fight you. To kill the competitor rather than be killed, start at the bottom. All successful companies in Silicon Valley followed this pattern.
13:40
The second element relates to customers. If you have a new technology, don’t go after an established market. Compete against non-consumption.
14:27
Example: Electronics and the transistor. From the late 1940s to early 1970s, consumer electronics used vacuum tubes. They were expensive and large, so only wealthy people could afford TVs.
15:13
Transistors were a disruptive technology but couldn’t immediately replace vacuum tubes. Established companies tried to make them good enough for existing products, investing billions to overcome technical barriers.
16:47
In 1955, Sony released a $2 pocket radio. It was small, static-filled, and limited in quality, but infinitely better than nothing. Teenagers loved it because it let them listen to music privately. In 1959, Sony introduced the first portable television for $99. It was limited but accessible, delighting customers who had no other option. Over time, solid-state electronics improved, and vacuum tube companies vanished.
19:46
Lesson: Target customers whose alternative is nothing. Then, improve products iteratively.
20:26
Today, electric vehicles illustrate the same principle. Tesla’s $100k cars compete with the best vehicles in California. But the bigger opportunity is targeting parents of teenagers who need slow, short-range cars—infinitely better than nothing.
21:49
Similarly, solar electricity is not competitive in developed markets due to grid reliability. But in Mongolia, half the population has no electricity. Cheap solar products are infinitely better than nothing, creating a booming new market across Africa and Asia.
24:53
Lesson: With new technologies, compete against non-consumption first to increase your probability of success.
25:38
Third theory: Jobs to be Done. Understand what job the customer is trying to accomplish. People don’t buy based on characteristics; they hire products to get a job done.
26:27
Example: Milkshakes. A fast-food chain tried improving milkshakes using customer demographics—it didn’t work. Observation revealed morning commuters bought milkshakes for long, boring drives.
30:29
Alternatives like bananas, donuts, bagels, and Snickers didn’t work as well. Milkshakes satisfied the job: filling, long-lasting, easy to consume while driving. Competitors were other ways to accomplish the job, not other milkshakes.
32:24
The job, not the customer, is the correct unit of analysis. Designing products around the job dramatically increases success probability.
33:06
Finally, venture capital itself needs disruption. When I started my first company in 1984, Bain Capital invested in Staples. Later, as funds grew, they moved upmarket to bigger deals. Entrepreneurs at the low end struggle to get funding due to this mismatch.
36:49
That concludes my prepared remarks. Now, you can ask me questions about how venture capital and entrepreneurship might get disrupted.

💡 **From Intuition to Architecture: How Product Design Matures**

In a 2013 talk, Clayton Christensen described how entire industries evolve — from *intuition*, to *patterns*, to *rules*.  

In the early days, the world’s best chemists at DuPont were like artists. They worked by intuition — mixing molecules, testing by feel, creating miracles like nylon and Kevlar through trial and error.  
Over decades, chemistry became teachable. Patterns emerged. Then rules. Then software.  
What once required a genius now needed a good foundation and the right tools.  

The same shift happens in every discipline — and product design is no exception.  

We started with intuition: a few gifted designers shaping experiences from instinct.  
Then came pattern libraries, design systems, and now tokens — our collective attempt to make design teachable, repeatable, and scalable.  

But here’s the paradox:  
Many teams have codified the *patterns* before ever understanding the *principles*.  

Just as medicine can’t jump from intuition to precision without first understanding the cause-and-effect in between, design can’t scale if it skips architecture — the connective tissue between business intent, technical systems, and user behavior.  

It’s not enough to move fast.  
We have to understand *why* things work — not just replicate *what* does.  

Because every mature system — in chemistry, medicine, or design — eventually faces the same question:  

Are we still experimenting, or have we started understanding?

**From Intuition to Architecture: What Clayton Christensen’s Talk Still Teaches Product Designers**

In 2013, Paul Adams warned us about *“The Dribbblisation of Design.”*  
He argued that design was becoming performative — aesthetics over architecture.  

A week ago, I revisited another timeless perspective — a talk by **Clayton Christensen**, the mind behind *Disruptive Innovation* and *Jobs to Be Done*.  
It’s a masterclass on how industries evolve: from *intuition → pattern recognition → rules-based understanding*.  

At first, the best designers — like DuPont’s early chemists — worked by feel.  
They mixed ideas like molecules, discovering through intuition and iteration.  
But as patterns emerged, knowledge became teachable, scalable, and structured.  

That’s exactly where **product design** stands today.  

Most teams still rely on intuition — talented designers “figuring it out” sprint by sprint.  
But design is maturing. We’re starting to see patterns:  
- repeatable flows,  
- reusable logic,  
- consistent mental models that map user behavior to system behavior.  

That’s **product architecture** — the moment when design stops being purely aesthetic and starts being a science of scalability.  

Christensen’s insight applies here:  
The goal isn’t to kill intuition; it’s to **codify it** — to turn what only a few can intuit into something the entire organization can execute consistently.  

That’s how design becomes *strategy*, not decoration.

---

💡 **From Intuition to Architecture: Why Product Design Needs Its “Scientific Revolution”**

In one of his rare talks, Clayton Christensen described how industries evolve from *intuition* → *patterns* → *rules*.  

Chemistry began with artists mixing molecules by hand — until they discovered repeatable patterns.  
Medicine evolved from intuition to empirical science.  
Even venture capital, he said, still behaves like “intuitive medicine” — where investors rely on gut feel instead of frameworks.  

And I couldn’t help thinking:  
**Product design is living through the same transformation.**

---

For years, design thrived on *intuition*.  
The best designers — like the early Dupont chemists — solved problems through taste, instinct, and a deep but unspoken sense of what “felt right.”  

But as products scale and complexity compounds, intuition alone doesn’t scale.  
We start needing **rules, architectures, and systems** — not to kill creativity, but to make it transferable, teachable, and reliable.  

That’s where design systems, component logic, and product architecture step in.  
They turn good intuition into reproducible outcomes — the same way chemistry became a science.  

---

Just like Christensen’s description of the organic chemistry revolution, our field is shifting:  

- **From art to pattern** → we learn reusable flows, principles, and heuristics.  
- **From pattern to system** → we codify them in design systems and architecture.  
- **From system to scalability** → we build infrastructure that outlives individual designers or teams.  

The beauty?  
Once that happens, design stops being an act of heroism — and becomes a reliable, evolving discipline.  

---

We’re not fully there yet.  
Many teams still run on “intuitive design” — every feature a new experiment, every flow reinvented, every project a reinvention of structure.  
But the next decade belongs to those who can **architect** design — who can turn intuition into infrastructure.  

That’s what made this Christensen talk timeless.  
He wasn’t just describing chemistry or startups.  
He was describing *us* — and the maturity curve every creative discipline must eventually climb

### From Intuition to Architecture

After Paul Adams’ *“The Dribbblisation of Design”*, I revisited another talk that feels just as relevant today — this time, from the late **Clayton Christensen**, the father of disruptive innovation.

In one of his rare talks, Christensen explains how every discipline evolves through the same three stages:

> **1. Intuitive stage** — mastered only by the few geniuses who can “feel” their way through.  
> **2. Pattern recognition stage** — where repetition reveals what works, and tacit knowledge becomes teachable.  
> **3. Rules-based stage** — where understanding becomes structured, predictable, and scalable.

He illustrates this through chemistry:  
What began as trial-and-error in DuPont’s labs — with scientists literally mixing atoms in beakers — eventually became pattern-based science, then predictive models.  
Now, any graduate with a laptop can design better molecules than the world’s top chemists from 50 years ago.

That same shift is happening across fields:  
Medicine evolving from intuition → evidence → precision.  
Venture capital moving (slowly) from gut instinct → pattern recognition.  
And **product design** — still in transition.

Most design teams today still operate in that **pattern stage** — learning from best practices, reusing UI kits, running usability tests.  
But few reach the **rules-based level**, where **product architecture**, **information hierarchy**, and **interaction logic** form a system that scales decisions instead of recreating them.

Christensen’s lesson echoes Paul Adams’:  
> “Without structure, success depends on the intuition of a few.  
> With structure, success becomes repeatable.”

If design wants to mature as an industry — not just evolve aesthetically — we need to codify our intuition into architecture.  
Because that’s how disciplines become scalable, teachable, and truly powerful.

🎥 Watch Christensen’s full talk here (Startup Grind, 2013):  
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RQSG_d0mmf0

**Why Most Product Teams Struggle to Build Something Truly New**  

In one of his lesser-known talks, the late **Clayton Christensen** described how industries evolve — from *trial and error* → *pattern recognition* → *rules and systems*.  

First it’s art, then it’s craft, and eventually, it becomes science.  

He told stories of how organic chemistry, medicine, and even venture capital went through this exact curve. What begins with intuition and luck, over time, becomes predictable — when people start seeing *patterns of success*.  

And the same is true for **product design**.  

In the early stages of a company, design is often intuitive — guided by instinct, taste, and speed. But as products grow, intuition alone becomes a bottleneck. Teams start repeating the same discussions, fixing the same UX problems, and scaling the same inconsistencies.  

That’s the signal that it’s time to move from **intuition to architecture** — from design-as-craft to **design-as-system**.  

Because just like chemistry matured through codified knowledge, design matures through **codified structure** — design systems, component logic, product architecture, and shared vocabulary between teams.  

The magic doesn’t disappear; it just becomes repeatable.  

Christensen also said something profound:  
> “To increase your probability of success, compete against non-consumption.”  

That line stuck with me.  
In product design, that means solving the job that no one else is solving — the invisible friction users learned to live with.  

That’s where real disruption starts — not in adding features, but in recognizing *what people hire your product to do*.

How to do a Product Critique
Watch and learn

Julie Zhuo
Julie Zhuo

Follow
6 min read
·
Jun 17, 2014
9.8K

22


All right, you caught me. The title of this article is a bit too fancy-pants. Product Critique is some dressed-up corporate lingo. It brings to mind whiteboards scrawled over with strong-smelling blue marker depicting arrows connecting abstract concepts like product-market fit and value proposition. It oozes I am an interview question, and while admittedly, it is my favorite thing to chat with candidates about, the language turns the whole thing into something much more formal than it ought to be.
Which is—in its simplest form—exploring the curiosity of why some products and experiences work for people, and why others don’t.
Listen, product design isn’t some innate skill one is born with, like having a good ear for distinguishing notes or possessing exceptionally powerful twitch muscles for sprinting across an Olympic stage. Developing good product intuition—by which I mean developing a good sixth sense about what features or experiences will resonate with people and become successful—is about two core tenets: 1) understanding people’s desires, and 2) understanding how people react to things.
Thankfully, all of us are people (except for those of us on the Internet who are dogs), and all of us react to things. So if you’re looking around for how to starting honing your product intuition, start with yourself and how you personally experience anything new.
As an example, let’s say you’re looking to try out a new app. You download it from the store and fire it up, ready to begin your product critique.
Hold up—before the loading screen even blinks into view for the first time, there’s a lot to consider:
How did this app come to your attention? Was it word of mouth from a friend? Interesting. Why’d she tell you about it? Or did you read about this app in an article? If so, what compelled you to actually go find it and download it? Was it recommended? Did it have a catchy icon and an intriguing name? Had you heard it about it before, and if so, how many times before? Why didn’t you download it then, and what eventually tipped you over towards trying it out now?
What’s your one-line summary of what this app does at this stage? It’s interesting to compare the answer to this question before using the app and after.
What’s the buzz so far? Do you have a sense of whether it’s popular? Whether it’s useful? Slick? Next-level? Did you happen to glance at the ratings, reviews, and description as you were downloading the app?
Thinking about the ways in which your first impressions of a new app are formed helps you better understand an app’s value proposition and marketing, and what the team behind it is doing—either implicitly or explicitly—to create that kind of impression.
Get Julie Zhuo’s stories in your inbox
Join Medium for free to get updates from this writer.

Subscribe
Now it’s time to open the app and play with it. Spend as much time as you would normally (which is probably more like a few minutes rather than half an hour), and ask yourself the following:
What’s the experience of getting started or signing up? Was it easy, with just a few button taps, or was it challenging with a bunch of verification steps?
How does this app explain itself in the first minute? Was it clear about what it did and how it works? Did the messaging feel friendly? Confusing? Did you read and retain the information, or did you skip it because it felt long-winded and boring?
How easy to use was the app? Did you understand immediately what the app was about, or did you need to tap around to try things and figure it out? Are there a lot of navigational items and buttons and gizmos to process, or did the entire thing feel familiar, contained and simple?
How did you feel while exploring the app? Did a cute illustration, funny quip, or piece of really interesting content make you smile? Did the navigation frustrate you because you couldn’t figure out how to get back to a previous screen? Did you feel smarter and more efficient for using this app? Did you take note of a particular detail and think Wow, I’ve never seen that before?
Did the app deliver on your expectations? Looking back to what you thought the app would do, did it match your experience of actually using it? If it’s a content app, was the content engaging? If it’s a utility app, did it solve the identified problem in a meaningful manner?
How long did you spend using the app? Time generally correlates with interest. If you spent a long time on the app, what about it kept you using it?
Just like with people, most opinions of a product are formed within the first few minutes. A quick run-through gives you a sense of whether the app actually provides value, is easy to use, and feels well-crafted.
After your first use of an app, the days and weeks following are just as important to consider broader questions of stickiness and growth:
How often have you used the app? When do you tend to use it? What compels you to open it? Is it because of enticing push notifications? Or because all your friends are still talking about and using it? Is it because you’ve found yourself relying on it again and again? Has this app transcended all obstacles to achieve the esteemed goal of becoming a regular habit in your life? Why or why not?
How does this app compare to other similar apps? Which things does it do better or worse? What would make you choose to use this app versus something similar?
What do other people think of this app? Getting additional perspectives is one of the quickest ways to learn about what works and what doesn’t in the broader market. Read reviews. Read comments in blogs. Read tweets about this app. Ask your friends what they think. Ask your cousins who live in a different town from you. Does their impression match yours? In what ways is it different, and why do you think it’s different?
Based on all that you know, how successful do you think the app will be a year from now? Take a real stance. Write it down in a digital sticky note somewhere. It can be private. You don’t have to shout it out to the world. But capturing a clear and honest bet so that you can go back and look to see if you were right or wrong is one of the most objective ways to combat hindsight bias.
(And eventually, after enough time has passed), were you right in your prediction of how this app was going to do? If not, why not? How were your own personal preferences and tastes similar or different from people in the broader market? You must understand this in order to better calibrate your opinions in the future.
There is no shortcut to developing better product instincts besides keen and close observation. By going through the above questions for everything you experience—using a new app, booking travel, standing in line at Disneyland, returning a package—you start to pick up on what details lead to what reactions.
Great experiences doesn’t just happen by happenstance. The best designers and product thinkers know people. They understand what motivates and what delights and what intrigues. They have strong theories about why any successful product or service is successful, and why any failed product or service has failed. They know this because they have been watching and studying people—including themselves—for a long, long time.
This process doesn’t have to be labeled a product critique. It doesn’t have to be a test or an interview question. It doesn’t have to happen because of any other person or obligatory cause.
It just has to happen because you’re curious, over and over and over again. Because you want to learn how to build good things.

---

## **The Weight of Compromise**

There’s a moment every designer eventually faces —  
when you realize your biggest challenge isn’t creativity, it’s **compromise**.

Not the glamorous kind that’s talked about in conference panels — “balancing business and user needs.”  
I’m talking about the real, everyday compromises that happen inside Jira tickets, sprint reviews, and budget meetings.  
The ones that slowly shape your craft in ways you never quite notice until you look back and realize:  
you’ve been designing around constraints for so long, you’ve started to internalize them.

---

When I first started designing, everything felt idealistic.  
I wanted to build seamless experiences — elegant, intuitive systems that made people’s lives better.  
But as the projects grew bigger, and the stakes higher, the reality became more complex.

At some point, **design stopped being about ideas**, and started being about **negotiations**.  
Negotiating with timelines. With backend limitations. With product owners who saw “user experience” as a layer on top, not the structure underneath.  
There were days when design critiques felt more like diplomatic briefings than creative sessions.

Each decision — whether it was a flow simplified for sprint scope, or a feature postponed “for phase two” — carried its own small weight.  
Individually, they seemed rational. Together, they started to define the boundaries of what we called “good enough.”

---

In environments where delivery velocity is the currency, **quality often becomes the silent cost**.  
You start hearing the same justifications on repeat:

> “We’ll improve it later.”  
> “Let’s just make it work for now.”  
> “The backend isn’t flexible enough yet.”

And maybe they’re right — sometimes, later *does* come.  
But more often, “later” becomes a graveyard of good intentions.

Still, I learned something important in all this: **compromise isn’t failure**.  
It’s inevitable. It’s the terrain of real product design.  
But there’s a difference between compromising *intentionally* and compromising *away* your principles.

---

True design maturity isn’t about avoiding compromise.  
It’s about developing the **judgment** to know which trade-offs strengthen the product — and which slowly hollow it out.

It’s about asking:  
Will this shortcut help us learn faster, or will it cement a bad habit into the system?  
Will this simplification serve the user, or just make our sprint metrics look better?

And sometimes, it’s about staying silent in the meeting — until the right moment — and saying one sentence that reframes the entire discussion.  
That’s design leadership. Not pixels. Not prototypes. Judgment.

---

Today, when I look back, I don’t just see features launched or interfaces shipped.  
I see **invisible decisions** — each one a negotiation between vision and reality.  
Some I’d change. Most, I wouldn’t.  
Because every compromise taught me to think more like an architect — someone who builds structures that *can evolve*, not just *look good* today.

That’s what real design is:  
not the art of perfection,  
but the discipline of building something **strong enough to survive imperfection**.

---

> _“I used to think great design was about pushing back.  
> Now I think it’s about knowing when to bend — and when bending would break the soul of the product.”_

After ten years as an entrepreneur, I started writing a blog called Startup Lessons Learned. My original goal was to provide support and encouragement to other entrepreneurs who, like me, had some unorthodox ideas about how to run companies. Along the way, I encountered two big surprises. They led me to a question I had never previously considered: is it possible that entrepreneurship is actually a management science?

For most of us, the phrase “management science” conjures up a decidedly non-entrepreneurial image, and for good reason. The preeminent management science, for much of the twentieth century was general management, pioneered by twentieth century giants like Peter Drucker and Alfred P. Sloan. As an entrepreneur, I often saw the best practices of general management fail startups. Applied out of context, they were dangerous.

This conflict has played out in many companies that I’ve worked with. My most recent startup created a marketplace for customers to buy and sell virtual goods for their 3D avatar. So you can imagine how I expected some skepticism when pitching ideas about technology innovation to, say, the U.S. Army. This was my first surprise: they understood that innovation needs to be understood at the level of principles, not just tactics.

Some tactics, like Continuous Deployment, are controversial, even among people with my background. But the really vexing questions came from entrepreneurs who inundated me with questions from other backgrounds. Could these techniques be used by enterprise software companies? Hardware manufacturers? Biotech startups?

Answering those questions requires understanding the principles of entrepreneurship in a rigorous way. I began to call this new methodology “the lean startup.” It is a rigorous application of lean principles to the problem of new product innovation.

Inspired by the lean manufacturing revolution (and excellent books like Lean Thinking), I started with a first fundamental question: in a startup, what activities are value-creating and which are waste? Usually, new projects are measured and held accountable to milestones and deadlines. When a project is on track, on time, and on budget, our intuition is that it is being well managed. This intuition is dead wrong.

Most startups fail because they are building something that nobody wants. Enamored with a new technology or a radical new product, many entrepreneurs never find a set of customers who will buy it. Each new feature added to such a product is actually wasted effort, even if it’s done on-time and on-budget. In product that nobody wants, all the features get thrown away.

This problem vexes venture-backed founders and general managers alike. Anyone who is tasked with creating disruptive innovation will find it familiar. In short, for an innovation on the wrong course, executing well doesn’t increase the odds of success. What’s needed, I realized, is a new definition of progress in a startup, one that recognizes that a startup’s primary mission is to penetrate the fog of the unknown and find out what their customers ultimately will want and accept. I call this unit of progress “validated learning about customers.” Because learning is the goal, the progress that startups make requires a very different kind of management.

This led me to a second surprise. As I was traveling the country talking to people about the lean startup, I kept meeting people in the audience who seemed out of place. They weren’t what we usually think of as entrepreneurs. They were general managers, most working in very large companies, who were tasked with creating new product innovations. They were smart, well-read, and understood Clay Christenson’s Innovator’s Solution cold.

They were adept at organizational politics: they knew how to form autonomous divisions with separate P&Ls, and could shield controversial or disruptive teams from meddling. And — my biggest surprise yet — they were visionaries. Like the startup founders I have worked with for years, they could see the future of their industries, and were prepared to take bold risks to seek out new and innovative solutions to the problems their companies would face.

They found the lean startup helpful. In fact, they considered it obvious that these principles — rapid iteration, a focus on validated learning, and reducing cycle time from idea to learning — applied to their situation. Here’s why. In my quest to put the practice of entrepreneurship on a rigorous footing, I had begun with this definition of a startup:

A startup is a human institution designed to create a new product or service under conditions of extreme uncertainty.




Originally, I used this definition to help entrepreneurs understand why the “best practices” of general management so often failed them. They can’t thrive when transplanted into the soil of extreme uncertainty that is the province of startups. But this definition is surprising: it doesn’t say anything about the size of the company, sector of the economy, or industry. Looking past my old preconceptions, I realized that entrepreneurs are everywhere: in government, in the occasional garage, and yes, in the traditional organization.

All entrepreneurs face the same fundamental challenges:

How do we know if we’re making progress?
How do we know if customers will want the product we are building?
And, if they do, how do we know what kind of value we can create with it?
But because every startup also strives to become an institution, answering these questions requires more than just disciplined thinking at the whiteboard. It requires the coordination of many different people, working in concert to answer them. In other words, it requires management.

The management challenges presented by entrepreneurship are different. For example, how do we hold an entrepreneurial team accountable for making progress? This is a core challenge faced by venture capitalists and corporate CFOs alike. A team might be making progress against their plan, might be hitting milestones, might even be earning revenue. But none of those artifacts constitute progress. Learning is progress. In short, it’s demonstrating the ability to use what we’ve learned to change customer behavior, with key metrics as the common source of evidence.

To measure learning requires a shift of attention from the output of models to their inputs. I’ll show you how to apply this to entrepreneurial situations in my next post.''

### 🧭 *“Entrepreneurship as a Management Science” — A Reflection on Eric Ries’ Early Writing*

When Eric Ries started his *Startup Lessons Learned* blog, he wasn’t trying to invent a movement.  
He was just trying to make sense of a pattern many of us have lived through —  
the moment when *execution excellence* becomes meaningless if you’re building something nobody wants.

What struck me reading this early essay wasn’t the familiar “lean startup” vocabulary,  
but how **relevant the core tension still is inside large organizations** today.

We still reward “on-time, on-budget” delivery.  
We still equate motion with progress.  
We still confuse the *appearance* of management with the *evidence* of learning.

Ries reframed that.  
He called startups “human institutions designed to create a new product or service under conditions of extreme uncertainty.”  
That definition changed everything for me —  
because it means innovation isn’t the opposite of management.  
It *requires* management — just a different kind.

One built on validated learning, not vanity metrics.  
On iteration speed, not illusion of control.  
On judgment, not just process.

It’s a mindset that belongs not only to founders,  
but also to **product teams inside established companies** —  
the ones quietly navigating uncertainty every day.

> “Learning is progress.”

Ten years later, that’s still the most radical sentence in business.

After ten years as an entrepreneur, I started writing a blog called Startup Lessons Learned. My original goal was to provide support and encouragement to other entrepreneurs who, like me, had some unorthodox ideas about how to run companies. Along the way, I encountered two big surprises. They led me to a question I had never previously considered: is it possible that entrepreneurship is actually a management science?

For most of us, the phrase “management science” conjures up a decidedly non-entrepreneurial image, and for good reason. The preeminent management science, for much of the twentieth century was general management, pioneered by twentieth century giants like Peter Drucker and Alfred P. Sloan. As an entrepreneur, I often saw the best practices of general management fail startups. Applied out of context, they were dangerous.

This conflict has played out in many companies that I’ve worked with. My most recent startup created a marketplace for customers to buy and sell virtual goods for their 3D avatar. So you can imagine how I expected some skepticism when pitching ideas about technology innovation to, say, the U.S. Army. This was my first surprise: they understood that innovation needs to be understood at the level of principles, not just tactics.

Some tactics, like Continuous Deployment, are controversial, even among people with my background. But the really vexing questions came from entrepreneurs who inundated me with questions from other backgrounds. Could these techniques be used by enterprise software companies? Hardware manufacturers? Biotech startups?

Answering those questions requires understanding the principles of entrepreneurship in a rigorous way. I began to call this new methodology “the lean startup.” It is a rigorous application of lean principles to the problem of new product innovation.

Inspired by the lean manufacturing revolution (and excellent books like Lean Thinking), I started with a first fundamental question: in a startup, what activities are value-creating and which are waste? Usually, new projects are measured and held accountable to milestones and deadlines. When a project is on track, on time, and on budget, our intuition is that it is being well managed. This intuition is dead wrong.

Most startups fail because they are building something that nobody wants. Enamored with a new technology or a radical new product, many entrepreneurs never find a set of customers who will buy it. Each new feature added to such a product is actually wasted effort, even if it’s done on-time and on-budget. In product that nobody wants, all the features get thrown away.

This problem vexes venture-backed founders and general managers alike. Anyone who is tasked with creating disruptive innovation will find it familiar. In short, for an innovation on the wrong course, executing well doesn’t increase the odds of success. What’s needed, I realized, is a new definition of progress in a startup, one that recognizes that a startup’s primary mission is to penetrate the fog of the unknown and find out what their customers ultimately will want and accept. I call this unit of progress “validated learning about customers.” Because learning is the goal, the progress that startups make requires a very different kind of management.

This led me to a second surprise. As I was traveling the country talking to people about the lean startup, I kept meeting people in the audience who seemed out of place. They weren’t what we usually think of as entrepreneurs. They were general managers, most working in very large companies, who were tasked with creating new product innovations. They were smart, well-read, and understood Clay Christenson’s Innovator’s Solution cold.

They were adept at organizational politics: they knew how to form autonomous divisions with separate P&Ls, and could shield controversial or disruptive teams from meddling. And — my biggest surprise yet — they were visionaries. Like the startup founders I have worked with for years, they could see the future of their industries, and were prepared to take bold risks to seek out new and innovative solutions to the problems their companies would face.

They found the lean startup helpful. In fact, they considered it obvious that these principles — rapid iteration, a focus on validated learning, and reducing cycle time from idea to learning — applied to their situation. Here’s why. In my quest to put the practice of entrepreneurship on a rigorous footing, I had begun with this definition of a startup:

A startup is a human institution designed to create a new product or service under conditions of extreme uncertainty.




Originally, I used this definition to help entrepreneurs understand why the “best practices” of general management so often failed them. They can’t thrive when transplanted into the soil of extreme uncertainty that is the province of startups. But this definition is surprising: it doesn’t say anything about the size of the company, sector of the economy, or industry. Looking past my old preconceptions, I realized that entrepreneurs are everywhere: in government, in the occasional garage, and yes, in the traditional organization.

All entrepreneurs face the same fundamental challenges:

How do we know if we’re making progress?
How do we know if customers will want the product we are building?
And, if they do, how do we know what kind of value we can create with it?
But because every startup also strives to become an institution, answering these questions requires more than just disciplined thinking at the whiteboard. It requires the coordination of many different people, working in concert to answer them. In other words, it requires management.

The management challenges presented by entrepreneurship are different. For example, how do we hold an entrepreneurial team accountable for making progress? This is a core challenge faced by venture capitalists and corporate CFOs alike. A team might be making progress against their plan, might be hitting milestones, might even be earning revenue. But none of those artifacts constitute progress. Learning is progress. In short, it’s demonstrating the ability to use what we’ve learned to change customer behavior, with key metrics as the common source of evidence.

To measure learning requires a shift of attention from the output of models to their inputs. I’ll show you how to apply this to entrepreneurial situations in my next post.''

That question became the foundation of what we now call *The Lean Startup* — one of the most quietly transformative frameworks in modern product development.

The principles that started in startups have now circled back to **corporates, governments, and institutions**.  
Because uncertainty isn’t a startup problem anymore — it’s a structural reality for everyone.

Are we *learning faster than uncertainty is changing?*

A shared obsession not with outputs, but with **progress that compounds through learning.**

### 214. **ASSISTANT / NOTE:**

That’s a great question — and it’s one that gets to the *core* of modern product thinking.  

Let’s unpack it clearly:  

---

### 💡 Whose idea is this?
This idea — that *entrepreneurship is a management science* — comes from **Eric Ries**, the author of **_The Lean Startup_** (2011).  

He built on the earlier work of **Steve Blank**, who introduced the *Customer Development* methodology — and combined it with agile software development principles. Together, their ideas reshaped how we think about building products under uncertainty.

Ries’s essay *“Is Entrepreneurship a Management Science?”* (and his later book) basically asked:  
> “Can we manage startups (or any uncertain initiative) with the same rigor that traditional businesses use — but in a way that fits high uncertainty and constant change?”

---

### ⚙️ What does it mean?
In classic management, success is measured by **efficiency, predictability, and execution**.  
But startups (and innovation teams inside corporations) operate under **extreme uncertainty** — they don’t yet know who their customer is, what the product should be, or what the market wants.

So Ries proposed a shift:
> Entrepreneurship should be treated as **a science of learning under uncertainty**, not as an art of guessing or a process of blind execution.

He introduced a new definition of progress:
- It’s not *building more features* or *shipping faster*.
- It’s *validated learning* — every iteration should test a hypothesis and bring us closer to what users actually need.

That’s where ideas like:
- **MVP (Minimum Viable Product)**  
- **Build–Measure–Learn loop**  
- **Pivot or Persevere**  
come from.

---

### 🧭 Why it matters (especially for you)
For someone like you — operating inside a large insurer such as Allianz — this idea is crucial because:
- You’re working on digital transformation inside an established structure.  
- You have to balance *efficiency* (corporate side) with *discovery and learning* (startup side).  

Ries’s thinking legitimizes that tension.  
It says innovation isn’t “creative chaos”; it’s **structured learning** managed with discipline and data.

So, when you design or test a new flow, run usability sessions, or iterate based on behavioral evidence — you’re not just “designing.”  
You’re *practicing the management science of entrepreneurship* within a corporate system.

Is it just good for you? Is it good for a business? Is it good for the world?

01:38

In our world — our increasingly quantified, digital world — it’s really popular, especially out in San Francisco, to talk about optimizing things to reach that highest peak.

What are we optimizing for?

They’d make this leap.

Because you can’t just describe the world and from that derive what you should be doing.

“X is natural; therefore, X is good.”

04:52

She reminded us that design isn’t just craft — it’s philosophy in motion.  
That every product decision hides a moral question: *What is good?*  
And that our obsession with optimization, metrics, and data often skips the one thing that gives design meaning — **the goal itself**.

> “The system won’t tell us what our objective should be.  
> First, we have to decide what’s good.”

That sentence hits differently today.

Because with AI, velocity, and experimentation at scale, it’s easier than ever to make things — and harder than ever to decide **why** we’re making them.

Design lives in the gap between *what is* and *what ought to be*.  
Our job isn’t just to ship screens, but to reconcile those two worlds — consciously, ethically, and with intention.

And as Hall said, the best tool for that isn’t software.  
It’s the question.

👉 *“Why?”*

Asking ‘’why’’? - November 2015
Erika Hall

TRANSCRIPT
00:03
Hello! Wow. I am incredibly, incredibly honored to be sharing the stage with the people I’ve seen so far today. Hi, I’m Erica Hall, and I’m the co-founder of Mule Design, as you heard.
So when John wrote to me and told me the theme, I was so excited — like, yeah, I’m right there.
00:27
Mule — we’ve got that. We’ve been doing that. I know that hybrid vigor.
And you see here, this is my dog, Rupert. He’s on theme. He’s half pug, half chihuahua — he’s a “Chug.” It’s true, it’s true.
And he’s an incredibly important part of my design process. He goes to work with me every day. He’s a good dog.
00:58
That was my test to make sure that my slides were actually working.
I won’t be talking specifically about much of our project work, but I will talk to you about the thread that runs through it all — one that really has to do with my background.
A designer’s job is to bring new things into the world. It’s an amazing job — a great job. And we hope good things.
We hope these things are all examples of good design. But this leads to the question: What is good?
How do you know it’s good?
Is it just good for you? Is it good for a business? Is it good for the world?
Is there such a thing as objectively good design?
01:38
This might sound like a really academic question — the kind of thing you talk about at a conference over drinks after seeing a new project launch — but I think it’s an incredibly important question.
Because the first rule of design is that everything follows from the goal.
And so, without a goal — without a good goal — I don’t think it’s possible to do good design.
In our world — our increasingly quantified, digital world — it’s really popular, especially out in San Francisco, to talk about optimizing things to reach that highest peak.
Because we can look at the numbers, count, tweak, and obsess.
But I always ask: Optimize for what?
What are we optimizing for?
The system won’t tell us. The design won’t tell us what our objective should be.
First, we have to decide what’s good.
02:35
There was once a Scotsman who thought quite a lot about how we decide what we ought to do — way back in the 1700s, in the middle of the 18th century.
This is David Hume — in his fancy hat.
He noticed a tendency thinkers had: to make claims about what you ought to do, what good you ought to pursue, based on what is.
They’d make this leap.
And I know we’re supposed to be bringing you new ideas, so I apologize — I’m bringing you something 300 years old.
But I think it’s really, really important.
Because you can’t just describe the world and from that derive what you should be doing.
One example of this is known as the naturalistic fallacy:
“X is natural; therefore, X is good.”
You see this a lot at Whole Foods — like, “Oh, animals don’t cook their food. That seems natural. I won’t cook my food.”
But cooking food is actually one of the things that contributed to our large brains — and it’s really good for us.
Plenty of things that aren’t natural are quite good.
Take an artificial heart — that’s a good thing.
Most people would agree it’s very good, because it comes from the principle that preserving life and health is a good thing.
You need to add that ethical principle — or some assumptions — to figure out what you should do with what you’ve learned about the world.
But the problem with value judgments and assumptions is that they’re up for debate.
04:15
Here’s another example of an “is–ought” problem in product design.
Getting around the city is very challenging.
We ought to invent an entirely new form of personal transportation.
This is the sort of “is–ought” leap the makers of the Segway made.
It had a fantastic, innovative design and great technology — but it wasn’t a commercial success, because there were other assumptions they didn’t examine.
Then we saw the Copenhagen Wheel — which took a much different way to proceed from this same observation about how the world is.
04:52
Fundamentally, design is a series of decisions.
And making decisions is very hard.
We do have to make some. We do have to commit — to a certain extent — to a path.
I agree with the synthesis. But a lot of times, to make progress, we have to make a decision.
I think this anxiety is behind so much of what we call data-driven design — because we hope that by looking at the data, we won’t have to make that judgment call.
We can just say, “Oh, I saw it in the numbers,” and that’ll tell us what we should do.
This — right here — is the “is–ought” problem.
It’s called Hume’s Law, or Hume’s Guillotine if you’re feeling a little studious.
The gap between what currently exists and what you’re aiming for — that’s where design happens.
Design is exactly the process of observing the world, having a vision for what the world should be, and often reconciling the differences between what different people need that world to be along the way.
And when we’re done — when we’re done with the design process — no matter how small, the world is different.
And we hope, better.
Because we hope we’ve chosen the good.
06:34
We’ve seen many people talk about this — about a world with easier biking, a world with more justice, a world with drink robots.
We’ve heard many fantastic examples of moving from this current state to some much better state through the power of design.
And so, what this means is that designers must also be philosophers.
Design requires both considering the world as it is and having a strong point of view on the world as it ought to be — and then making a plan to get there.
07:18
A philosopher is someone who strives for systematic expertise about the nature of reality — and it seems to me that this expertise is a prerequisite for doing design.
I think I’m stealing this from Bertrand Russell, a great British philosopher.
Actually, I listen to the History of Philosophy while I run — another hybrid activity!
I really feel like I’m maximizing — it’s true.
I listen to this pleasant British reader talking about Kant, and I’m like, “I’m running the line!” It’s really — I feel very integrated in that moment.
So, design exists in the gap between science and speculation.
We start with what we know, and then we think about what might possibly be.
That’s exactly the place where design lives — between the unknowable future we’re trying to get to and what we know now — and we think about how various solutions might bring us closer.
08:17
The handy thing about being a hybrid designer and philosopher is that the uniform is the same.
This is my Casual Friday — and it also works if you’re going to be James Bond too!
For me, studying philosophy was a beautiful accident with very practical results.
No philosophers showed up on career day at my high school.
I initially really wanted to be an architect. I used to make house plans — little layouts on my Etch A Sketch.
I even got the door curves right and everything.
But then I had this really sadistic English teacher who made us all read The Fountainhead.
I don’t know if you’ve had to read that — but yeah, then I was done.
Then I thought, “Oh, maybe Supreme Court Justice — that sounds like an awesome career.”
I went to Taft High and thought, “Oh, being a Supreme Court Justice — that’s a cool job, where you get to consider the world and make really important discernments.”
But then I realized I had just as much chance of being a professional basketball player as a Supreme Court Justice.
09:29
That same teacher had this great parlor game — he’d look around the classroom and discern what our careers would be.
He’d look at someone and say, “Teacher. Writer. Actor. Lawyer.”
When he got to me, he said, “I don’t know. I can’t tell what you’re going to do.”
So I said, “Okay, well, I guess I’ll study liberal arts.”
And I think the reason he couldn’t tell was because, at that point, the Internet was barely a thing.
It was still an NSF project — the web hadn’t even come into existence yet.
So I went off and studied philosophy. I had the good luck to be in a great department with a lot of excellent, strong women professors.
I had great role models and learned fantastic tools — to keep my inquiry sharp.
And unlike what Fred said, I actually use my degree every single day — because it turns out that philosophy and the Internet are a very important match.
10:34
So, I’m a designer — at least that’s what it says on my passport application, so it must be true.
But I’m a designer with no obvious craft.
My craft is my critique.
My craft is building a case, building an argument, imagining a world of abstract concepts.
I work with a team that’s very, very good at the craft part — because you really need the two together.
But the craft, I don’t think, is sufficient without that framework.
A colleague of mine, Thomas Wendt, wrote a fantastic book using the philosophy of Heidegger to talk about experience design.
He said, “We make an excellent job of developing products but a terrible job of designing them.”
Because he, too, was concerned that people defined design purely as craft.
11:32
That’s a real lowest-common-denominator way of looking at it — but it has a pull.
When we just think, “Am I good enough at the craft?”
Fortunately, there have been great advances — design thinking in businesses, RISD actually having a philosophy department as well as being a design school.
But I even talk to designers who are looking for jobs, and they tell me the first thing recruiters ask them is, “What tool do you use?”
They don’t ask, “What’s your quality of thought? What’s your framework? What’s your approach?”
So much of what we consider design — and our methods for evaluating design, especially for digital products and services — are based on graphic and industrial design, on a surface that doesn’t really apply anymore.
12:03
If good design is what best meets the goal — then what’s good design?
Take something like Craigslist. It’s been around for 20 years as a digital product. It’s enduring and fantastic.
But a graphic designer might say, “It’s not very good.”
Wikipedia has a very similar look — very simple — but it’s perfect for rapidly updating information.
So you have to ask: What creates enduring value?
Look at Airbnb — I love Airbnb. I’ve stayed with them. They use visual design to help create trust between people, and they’re famous for having designer-founders.
But recently in San Francisco, they put up billboards chiding the city for perhaps not spending the tax money they’d gotten from Airbnb well.
So this calls into question — they have that surface design, but do they have that deep framework in pursuing the idea of community?
13:23
Design problems are philosophical problems.
The practice of philosophy changes as we gain new knowledge — and the practice of design changes with technology.
In the 1970s, American philosopher Robert Nozick came up with the idea of the Experience Machine.
He said: if psychologists could hook you up to a machine that could totally simulate any pleasurable experience you wanted — would that be good?
If having a pleasant time were the highest good, maybe it would be.
But he argued that people wouldn’t want to plug into this machine — because they have other values.
Well, we come to the present, and it turns out we didn’t need demonic psychologists to invent this machine for us — Apple did.
And we don’t need to do a thought experiment anymore — because we can see how compellingly we’re pulled into this somewhat synthesized world.
Thanks to digital technology, the space between thought and artifact has collapsed.
And this means it’s even more important, as designers, to make conscious, intentional choices — because there’s less and less friction between idea and action.
Is this a good thing or a bad thing?
That’s a judgment we have to make based on our values.
14:56
For over a billion people, Facebook is an intermediary in our most intimate relationships.
And with their real-name policy, they’re making a strong philosophical statement about authentic identity.
It comes from a good place — from a play for safety.
But the truth is, out in the world, there are people who would be made less safe by using their real names online — and who actually have an identity they consider more authentic than what’s on their bill or driver’s license.
15:47
Digital design is changing the nature of our human relationships.
It’s changing dating, finance, even dealing with our relatives, our children, education, and knowledge.
We’re not dealing with physical objects anymore — we’re dealing with pure ideas.
We forget this because we cloak these ideas in metaphors: the illusion of buttons, the illusion of pages, the illusion of folders or photo albums.
The object-permanence part of our brain tricks us into thinking our browser tabs are just 5,000 infinitely thin slices of paper.
But what we’re dealing with are pure ideas.
And the best tool to work with ideas is the question.
16:49
The designer’s most important tool is the question.
The fantastic thing about deciding to be a philosopher as well as a designer is that you can create this path — you can create these questions.
But you have to move your definition of design a little bit.
We have to move from thinking about the how to thinking about the why.
The “how” is very comfortable — we can master the how.
But the “why” is something we have to continually ask.
We can never stop asking why.
It’s a scary journey into the unknown — and that’s the most exciting part of design.
Thank you.
[Applause]

### 🔹 Draft: *“The most timeless talk on asking ‘why’”*

Back in 2015, **Erika Hall** gave one of the most important talks in design:  
**“Asking Why.”**

She reminded us that *design isn’t just craft* — it’s *philosophy applied to the real world.*

We often talk about design as if it’s just a set of methods, tools, or polished screens.  
But Hall goes deeper:  
> “Design exists in the gap between what is and what ought to be.”  

That line changes everything.  
It means our job is not just to observe the world, but to decide what *should* exist — and why.

And that’s where I think product design and philosophy overlap.  
Both require judgment under uncertainty.  
Both demand asking, *“What’s good? What’s progress?”* before chasing optimization.

Today, in an era where “AI-assisted design” can generate a hundred variations in seconds,  
this talk feels more relevant than ever.  
Because speed without judgment doesn’t create value — it just amplifies confusion.

Hall closes with a reminder every designer, manager, and founder should revisit:

> “The designer’s most important tool is the question.  
> We have to move from thinking about the how to thinking about the why.”  

If you haven’t seen it, it’s one of the most timeless talks on design thinking, ethics, and clarity:

🎥 *“Asking Why” — Erika Hall (2015)*  
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RQSG_d0mmf0  

---

Would you like me to make a **shorter version (under 8 lines)** too — something that feels tighter and more LinkedIn-native (for better engagement while keeping the reflection)?

00:58
That was my test to make sure that my slides were actually working.
I won’t be talking specifically about much of our project work, but I will talk to you about the thread that runs through it all — one that really has to do with my background.
A designer’s job is to bring new things into the world. It’s an amazing job — a great job. And we hope good things.

01:38

What are we optimizing for?

02:35

They’d make this leap.
And I know we’re supposed to be bringing you new ideas, so I apologize — I’m bringing you something 300 years old.
But I think it’s really, really important.
Because you can’t just describe the world and from that derive what you should be doing.
One example of this is known as the naturalistic fallacy:

You see this a lot at Whole Foods — like, “Oh, animals don’t cook their food. That seems natural. I won’t cook my food.”

04:15

04:52
Fundamentally, design is a series of decisions.

I think this anxiety is behind so much of what we call data-driven design — because we hope that by looking at the data, we won’t have to make that judgment call.
We can just say, “Oh, I saw it in the numbers,” and that’ll tell us what we should do.
This — right here — is the “is–ought” problem.
It’s called Hume’s Law, or Hume’s Guillotine if you’re feeling a little studious.
The gap between what currently exists and what you’re aiming for — that’s where design happens.
Design is exactly the process of observing the world, having a vision for what the world should be, and often reconciling the differences between what different people need that world to be along the way.
And when we’re done — when we’re done with the design process — no matter how small, the world is different.
And we hope, better.
Because we hope we’ve chosen the good.
06:34
We’ve seen many people talk about this — about a world with easier biking, a world with more justice, a world with drink robots.
We’ve heard many fantastic examples of moving from this current state to some much better state through the power of design.
And so, what this means is that designers must also be philosophers.
Design requires both considering the world as it is and having a strong point of view on the world as it ought to be — and then making a plan to get there.
07:18

I think I’m stealing this from Bertrand Russell, a great British philosopher.

I really feel like I’m maximizing — it’s true.
I listen to this pleasant British reader talking about Kant, and I’m like, “I’m running the line!” It’s really — I feel very integrated in that moment.
So, design exists in the gap between science and speculation.
We start with what we know, and then we think about what might possibly be.
That’s exactly the place where design lives — between the unknowable future we’re trying to get to and what we know now — and we think about how various solutions might bring us closer.
08:17
The handy thing about being a hybrid designer and philosopher is that the uniform is the same.
This is my Casual Friday — and it also works if you’re going to be James Bond too!
For me, studying philosophy was a beautiful accident with very practical results.
No philosophers showed up on career day at my high school.
I initially really wanted to be an architect. I used to make house plans — little layouts on my Etch A Sketch.
I even got the door curves right and everything.
But then I had this really sadistic English teacher who made us all read The Fountainhead.
I don’t know if you’ve had to read that — but yeah, then I was done.
Then I thought, “Oh, maybe Supreme Court Justice — that sounds like an awesome career.”
I went to Taft High and thought, “Oh, being a Supreme Court Justice — that’s a cool job, where you get to consider the world and make really important discernments.”
But then I realized I had just as much chance of being a professional basketball player as a Supreme Court Justice.
09:29
That same teacher had this great parlor game — he’d look around the classroom and discern what our careers would be.
He’d look at someone and say, “Teacher. Writer. Actor. Lawyer.”

So I said, “Okay, well, I guess I’ll study liberal arts.”
And I think the reason he couldn’t tell was because, at that point, the Internet was barely a thing.
It was still an NSF project — the web hadn’t even come into existence yet.
So I went off and studied philosophy. I had the good luck to be in a great department with a lot of excellent, strong women professors.

10:34
So, I’m a designer — at least that’s what it says on my passport application, so it must be true.
But I’m a designer with no obvious craft.
My craft is my critique.
My craft is building a case, building an argument, imagining a world of abstract concepts.
I work with a team that’s very, very good at the craft part — because you really need the two together.
But the craft, I don’t think, is sufficient without that framework.
A colleague of mine, Thomas Wendt, wrote a fantastic book using the philosophy of Heidegger to talk about experience design.
He said, “We make an excellent job of developing products but a terrible job of designing them.”
Because he, too, was concerned that people defined design purely as craft.
11:32
That’s a real lowest-common-denominator way of looking at it — but it has a pull.
When we just think, “Am I good enough at the craft?”
Fortunately, there have been great advances — design thinking in businesses, RISD actually having a philosophy department as well as being a design school.
But I even talk to designers who are looking for jobs, and they tell me the first thing recruiters ask them is, “What tool do you use?”
They don’t ask, “What’s your quality of thought? What’s your framework? What’s your approach?”
So much of what we consider design — and our methods for evaluating design, especially for digital products and services — are based on graphic and industrial design, on a surface that doesn’t really apply anymore.
12:03
If good design is what best meets the goal — then what’s good design?
Take something like Craigslist. It’s been around for 20 years as a digital product. It’s enduring and fantastic.
But a graphic designer might say, “It’s not very good.”
Wikipedia has a very similar look — very simple — but it’s perfect for rapidly updating information.
So you have to ask: What creates enduring value?
Look at Airbnb — I love Airbnb. I’ve stayed with them. They use visual design to help create trust between people, and they’re famous for having designer-founders.
But recently in San Francisco, they put up billboards chiding the city for perhaps not spending the tax money they’d gotten from Airbnb well.
So this calls into question — they have that surface design, but do they have that deep framework in pursuing the idea of community?
13:23
Design problems are philosophical problems.
The practice of philosophy changes as we gain new knowledge — and the practice of design changes with technology.
In the 1970s, American philosopher Robert Nozick came up with the idea of the Experience Machine.
He said: if psychologists could hook you up to a machine that could totally simulate any pleasurable experience you wanted — would that be good?
If having a pleasant time were the highest good, maybe it would be.
But he argued that people wouldn’t want to plug into this machine — because they have other values.
Well, we come to the present, and it turns out we didn’t need demonic psychologists to invent this machine for us — Apple did.
And we don’t need to do a thought experiment anymore — because we can see how compellingly we’re pulled into this somewhat synthesized world.
Thanks to digital technology, the space between thought and artifact has collapsed.
And this means it’s even more important, as designers, to make conscious, intentional choices — because there’s less and less friction between idea and action.
Is this a good thing or a bad thing?
That’s a judgment we have to make based on our values.
14:56
For over a billion people, Facebook is an intermediary in our most intimate relationships.
And with their real-name policy, they’re making a strong philosophical statement about authentic identity.
It comes from a good place — from a play for safety.
But the truth is, out in the world, there are people who would be made less safe by using their real names online — and who actually have an identity they consider more authentic than what’s on their bill or driver’s license.
15:47
Digital design is changing the nature of our human relationships.
It’s changing dating, finance, even dealing with our relatives, our children, education, and knowledge.
We’re not dealing with physical objects anymore — we’re dealing with pure ideas.
We forget this because we cloak these ideas in metaphors: the illusion of buttons, the illusion of pages, the illusion of folders or photo albums.
The object-permanence part of our brain tricks us into thinking our browser tabs are just 5,000 infinitely thin slices of paper.
But what we’re dealing with are pure ideas.
And the best tool to work with ideas is the question.
16:49
The designer’s most important tool is the question.
The fantastic thing about deciding to be a philosopher as well as a designer is that you can create this path — you can create these questions.
But you have to move your definition of design a little bit.
We have to move from thinking about the how to thinking about the why.
The “how” is very comfortable — we can master the how.
But the “why” is something we have to continually ask.
We can never stop asking why.
It’s a scary journey into the unknown — and that’s the most exciting part of design.
Thank you.
[Applause]
