Every product, every feature, every redesign carries a story. If I can’t explain the *why* and *value* in a single page, in one concise pitch, I know it’s not ready. Complexity doesn’t impress — clarity does.  

Design isn’t just screens or interactions. It’s about creating understanding, guiding attention, shaping decisions. And just like a 15-second pitch, that requires ruthless clarity.  

💡 **Question for you:** How do you simplify complex ideas in your work so people *get it instantly*?

UX: Back to the future

Rebecca Grier
Rebecca Grier

Follow
10 min read
·
Dec 12, 2023
7



A list of classic texts in behavioural science, human factors, and similar for those looking to improve their knowledge of UX.
TL/DR: A colleague said to me, “when you retire, I want your library.” Based on that comment, I decided to compile a reading list for those in UX. As I obtained my Ph.D. in Human Factors Psychology nearly 20 years ago, these are classic texts. Each entry has a brief description of why I added it to the list.
Don’t Make Me Think by S. Krug
Psychology (Design) of Everyday Things by D. Norman
Set Phasers on Stun by S. Casey & The Atomic Chef by S. Casey
Thinking Fast & Slow by D. Kahneman
Quantifying the User Experience by J. Sauro
Questionnaire Construction Manual & Annex by Babbitt & Nystrom
Cheaper by the Dozen by F. Gilbreth & E. Gilbreth Carey (with bonus film “Desk Set”)
Introduction to Human Factors Engineering by C. Wickens et al.
Improving Function Allocation for Integrated Systems Design by D. Beevis, P. Essens, & H. Schuffel
Various Standards & Guidelines
The Icon Book By W. Horton
HCI Beyond the GUI by P. Kortum
1. Don’t Make Me Think by S. Krug
I’m starting this UX reading list with Steve Krug’s “Don’t make me think: A common sense approach to web usability.” There are new editions of this book, which I have not read. The original is written in a style that exalts the principles of UX through demonstration. It is also a quick read and written for the UX professional or for management. You will gain an appreciation for the very basics of UX in the digital age.
2. Psychology (Design) of Everyday Things by D. Norman
The second entry in this UX reading list is the classic Psychology of Everyday Things, by Don Norman. Later editions of this book had a change in title to The Design of Everyday Things. I prefer the original title for two reasons. First the acronym is much more elegant P.O.E.T.. Second, I am a psychologist by training.
Don Norman also has a Ph.D. in Psychology. He also was one of the early leaders in human-computer interaction as it related to the ubiquitous GUI. I think the title change occurred around the same time as the term “design thinking” came into vogue, but I could be wrong.
Either way, Norman uses case studies to illustrate how the design of everything impacts the thoughts and actions of users. Via these case studies he introduces the concepts of affordances, gibsonian/ecological psychology, mental models, and other topics within cognitive/perceptual psychology. These case studies elucidate the point that blaming the user is a wrong strategy. Also the interested reader can apply the lessons of these cases to completely different situations. Though POET is longer than the first entry (Don’t Make Me Think — Krug), it is another quick read. Therefore a great starting point for those interested in UX as a career or wondering why it is important to the development of technology.
3. Set Phasers on Stun by S. Casey & The Atomic Chef by S. Casey
The 3rd entry has 2 books, both by Steven Casey. Both books are collections of case studies in which the design of a system led people to make errors. Like the previous entries (“Don’t Make Me Think” & “The Psychology of Everyday Things”), these books are quick reads written for a general audience. Unlike the first two, there is no analysis. The case studies lay out the facts that the human errors were the result of the system design. If I was leading a class, I would assign students to read the case studies and think (1) is it right to blame the people in the stories and (2) what steps could have been taken to prevent these errors.
4. Thinking Fast & Slow by D. Kahneman
So far, this UX reading list has focused on books for a general audience. This entry is no different. However, you may not initially see its link to UX.
Get Rebecca Grier’s stories in your inbox
Join Medium for free to get updates from this writer.

Subscribe
“Thinking Fast & Slow,” by Nobel laureate Daniel Kahneman accurately summarizes what is known about human cognition. Though the book doesn’t mention UX or technology design, all of the concepts in this book have been discussed in the previous books. In “Psychology of Everyday Things,” Norman discusses Gibsonian psychology & affordances — this is the pattern recognition that defines Kahneman’s “thinking fast.” Norman’s 7 stages of action are Kahneman’s “thinking slow.” Casey’s “Set Phasers on Stun” & “The Atomic Chef” tell the stories of what happens when designs wrongly stimulate “thinking fast.” Krug’s “Don’t Make Me Think” tells how to take advantage of “thinking fast” to reduce people’s frustrations.
5. Quantifying the User Experience by J. Sauro
The four previous entries in the UX reading list have been focused on books for the general audience. This entry is written specifically for the UX researcher/practitioner. In “Quantifying the User Experience,” Jeff Sauro has created a practical guide to the topic. Most text books on the topic of research methods/ design of experiments and statistics are very theoretical and philosophical. These books have their place. “Quantifying the User Experience” describes the more practical concerns associated with these topics in very readable text. Though it is readable, it is not dumbed-down. If you are a UX practitioner who has never had a course work in psychological research methods or statistics for the social sciences, I encourage you to read this book. If you have had these courses, I encourage you to keep a copy on your desk as reference material. I find myself turning to it when I need to convince reluctant stakeholders of the best path forward.
6. Questionnaire Construction Manual & Annex by Babbitt & Nystrom
This entry goes in to more detail on quantitative UX research methods, specifically surveys. Many people believe that writing a survey is simple and it is what one chooses to do when they can think of no other way to measure/research/test a phenomenon. Neither of these are the case. A survey is a way to quantify people’s thoughts so they can be statistically analysed.
I have taught many people about survey design and administration best practices. Though there are numerous books on psychometrics that I use to develop these courses, Babbitt & Nystrom is by far the most thorough reference on the topic. If there is a question about survey design, they have done literature review and empirical research on that question.
The one limitation is that it was written in the late 1980s — so it does not address technology specific questions. Regardless, it is still my first reference when I have a question about survey design. Most notably, they did research to identify response labels for Likert-like questions that are equal intervals. This is important to ensure the data from the responses can be treated as parametric for inferential statistics.
6. Cheaper by the Dozen by F. Gilbreth & E. Gilbreth Carey (with bonus film “Desk Set”)
This entry is a bit of a diversion from the others because “Cheaper by the Dozen” is a semi-autobiographical novel written in 1950 that on its surface appears to have no connection to UX. That said it is on the list because there is a connection; I promise.
Frank Gilbreth Jr. and Ernestine Gilbreth Carey penned a loving tribute describing their lives as two of the dozen children raised by Frank and Lillian Gilbreth in the early 1900s. How does this relate to UX? Frank and Lillian Gilbreth are two of the pioneers of the integration of psychology and engineering. This integration is the heart of human factors, human computer interaction, and UX. Frank and Lillian used the principles of this nascent discipline to create a fun and efficient home life for their 11 children while being very busy working parents. Interspersed with anecdotes of children being children in the early 20th century, are a lot of great tidbits about how UX best practices came to be best practices. It is a quick and light read that I highly recommend for anyone in UX to know the founders of the discipline.
To further beat back the idea that UX is a 21st century creation, I also encourage you to set aside time to watch, “Desk Set,” which is a Spencer Tracy- Katherine Hepburn rom-com. Tracy plays a character based on someone whose work is similar to Frank Gilbraith. Hepburn plays a librarian, who fears she is being replaced by a machine. In addition to the great chemistry and acting from the pair, there are a lot of best practices of the UX discipline sprinkled throughout the story.
7. Introduction to Human Factors Engineering by C. Wickens et al.
This book is my go-to UX reference. There are 19 chapters covering the vast majority of questions related to human-system interaction from how to design research and system evaluation to design a variety of systems for usability. Furthermore, it goes into the WHY behind these best practices so that an individual knows when and how to bend the best practices. I refer to the 13 (visual) display principles frequently. The chapters on decision making, human computer interaction, workload, and safety provide a clear connection between the topics in Kahneman’s Thinking Fast and Slow (entry #4) and their application to UX. It is easily one of the most readable textbooks I have encountered. It reviews the scientific research literature accurately but clearly for non-scientists.
8. Improving Function Allocation for Integrated Systems Design by D. Beevis, P. Essens, & H. Schuffel
It is a truism, that as tasks become more automated the role of the human changes. When changing the way an outcome is achieved, we need to make sure that the changes improve the efficiency, effectiveness, and satisfaction of the human (i.e., ISO 9241–11 definition of usability). In my experience the best way to do this is the through task analysis and function allocation. These methods are very similar to the “jobs to be done theory.” The first step is to define the outcomes of performing a certain “job/task.” Task analysis and function allocation help to identify the sub-outcomes that are needed to occur to complete this “job.” Function allocation was first described by Paul Fitts in the early 1950s where the Fitts’ list described the things that humans are better at and the things that machines are better at. Though those as technology has advanced the components of each list have changed, considering what functions need to be completed and the best way of completing those is still critical to user experience.
To that end I have included “Improving Function Allocation for Integrated Systems Design by D. Beevis, P. Essens, & H. Schuffel” as the 9th entry on the UX reading list. It is a compilation of papers (written by both program managers and engineers) describing different approaches to and the benefits from function allocation. I encourage all UX professionals to become familiar with the concepts of task analysis and function allocation. This text is probably the best compilation of information on this topic.
For more information on Fitts’ List and it’s author Paul Fitts, listen to this episode of Design Critique, https://www.designcritique.net/podcasts/wordcast-paul-fitts-his-law-and-his-list/.
9. Standards & Guidelines
One of the best resources for UX professionals are the wide variety of standards that exist. These standards are based on research that has been conducted in a wide variety of contexts. It is always best to do desk (secondary) research by reviewing standards and best practices (even in other industries) before conducting primary research. Here is a list of some of my go to standards & guidelines resources:
· MIL-STD-1472G — Amongst the most comprehensive pieces of design guidance out there. It covers almost every conceivable user experience one can think of from standard GUIs to speech interfaces; from vibrations to lighting; from foot pedals to virtual reality; and excellent anthropomorphic data. The US military uses almost every conceivable piece of technology for almost every conceivable purpose (vehicles to medical; word processing & timecard software to nuclear reactors). Seriously this is ALWAYS the first place I look. http://everyspec.com/MIL-STD/MIL-STD-1400-1499/download.php?spec=MIL-STD-1472G.039997.pdf
· Usability.gov — high level software UX process and design guidance. One thing I love about this document is that it provides strength of evidence and importance for following.
· Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) — Though written for the web- they apply to most user interfaces. Also though they are labelled accessibility guidelines they are really inclusivity guidance that make your user interfaces better for everyone! http://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/
· Section 508 — The US law for IT & communication accessibility. If WCAG doesn’t cover it and it is IT & communications related, Section 508 does. https://www.access-board.gov/guidelines-and-standards/communications-and-it/about-the-section-508-standards/section-508-standards
· NISTIR 7889 — National Institute of Standards (NIST) wrote a comprehensive list of standards for Department of Homeland Security. If you want to familiarize yourself with what UX standards exist, this is a great starting point. https://www.cpsc.gov/s3fs-public/HF-Standard-Practice-Draft-12Feb2018.pdf?CGk4Zs9GabjCnZ5RXQuSlr2toQ1aLPhJ
· Guidance on Application of Human Factors to Consumer Products — A joint effort between US & Canada’s Consumer Product agencies to define best practices for designing usable systems. https://www.cpsc.gov/s3fs-public/HF-Standard-Practice-Draft-12Feb2018.pdf?CGk4Zs9GabjCnZ5RXQuSlr2toQ1aLPhJ
· Summary of Many Relevant ISO Standards — The Human Factors and Ergonomics Society has summaries of numerous ISO standards that are pertinent to UX. https://www.hfes.org/resources/technical-standards
11. The Icon Book by W. Horton
A critical component of most user interfaces are icons. Badly designed icons can lead to poor user experience by creating features that are hidden (i.e., difficult to find) or confusion as to how to access features. Both of which can impact the usability and user experience of the technology. William Horton deftly walks the reader through when and when not to use icons and the icon design process. There are numerous examples that illustrate the principles being written about. Anyone involved in the process of system design could benefit from this book.
12. HCI Beyond the GUI by P. Kortum
The twelth item on the UX Reading List is Phil Kortum’s “HCI Beyond the GUI.” Each chapter of the book details an interface category (e.g., Haptic, Speech, etc..) and documents what best practices exist for design and testing of that interface. This book is intended for the UX practitioner or student. Like the fifth entry, Sauro’s “Quantifying the User Experience,” this book is a reference on my shelf that I turn to when I need to convince a stakeholder that it isn’t just my opinion, but research exists on the topic.

---

### 3. *“How to Specify the Participant Group Size for Usability Studies: A Practitioner’s Guide”* (2009)  
From the Journal of Usability Studies — gives a grounding in how many test users are needed under which conditions. (Mentioned in JUS Top 10 list) citeturn0search2  
**Why share:** Many product teams ignore rigor in usability testing; this offers a scientific but practical baseline.

---

### 4. *“DUX2005: One Person’s Journey”* by Elizabeth Bacon (2005)  
A reflective, on-the-ground conference writeup about how UX practitioners think and evolve over time. citeturn0search0  
**Why share:** It’s a candid look at how UX practice matures — good for more junior designers and for reminding senior folks of the journey.

---

### 5. *“Design Thinking”* by Tim Brown (2008)  
One of the early canonical articles bringing “design thinking” into business strategy discourse. citeturn0search1  
**Why share:** Many people quote “design thinking” but forget its origins and the challenges of integrating it in real organizations.

---

### 6. *“Ubiquitous Computing User Experience Design”* (2008) by Mike Kuniavsky  
An early take on UX in the world of IoT, smart devices, and ambient computing — arguing UX must evolve beyond screens. citeturn0news21  
**Why share:** We live in that world today — this article helps trace how UX thinking had to catch up.  

---

### 7. *“Case Study Research: An Essential Ingredient of Thought Leadership”* (2008)  
Though more in the domain of strategy / consulting, it defends using deep case research rather than superficial surveys. citeturn0search5  
**Why share:** In product/design work, many insights are buried in narratives, not data tables. This supports publishing with depth.

---

### 8. *“The Design of Business: Why Design Thinking is the Next Competitive Advantage”* (2009) by Roger Martin  
Not an article, but a seminal book that introduced the “knowledge funnel” (mystery → heuristic → algorithm). citeturn0search20  
**Why share:** As companies scale, much of design becomes systematized. This helps map the transition from art → design → process.

---

### 9. *Socio-Technical Design / Enid Mumford* (2000 / earlier)  
While older than 10 years, her work on designing systems that balance people and technology remains under-cited in modern UX/DSD discussions. citeturn0search26  
**Why share:** Especially in regulated or enterprise environments, understanding the social + technical interplay is a huge lever.

---

### 10. *“Market-Oriented Cloud Computing: Vision, Hype, and Reality for Delivering IT Services as Computing Utilities”* (2008)  
This early paper laid out visions of cloud, SLA-driven service, and resource markets. citeturn0academia23  
**Why share:** Many product teams now build on cloud assumptions; revisiting early thinking illuminates how much was visionary vs oversold.

---

Designing Technology with the Human Mind in Mind: Part 4

Rebecca Grier
Rebecca Grier

Follow
11 min read
·
Jan 23, 2024
109



Workload, Stress, & Total System Performance
Intro: This is the 4th in a series of articles to discuss what behavioural science knows about human cognition for those in product development. The 1st article explained why product makers should understand human cognition and introduced the dual system model of cognition (aka “Thinking Fast & Slow”). The 2nd article dove deeper into one part of that dual system model, “The filter.” The 3rd article introduced Working Memory. This article dives deeper into into cognitive workload & stress and how they impact performance. Future articles will discuss leadership, motivation, among other topics. All articles will explain why this knowledge is important to making technology that has a great user experience.
What is cognitive workload?
To understand cognitive workload one first must understand the dual system model of cognition, which I described in the first 3 articles. Briefly, all information that is sensed by the human sensory systems passes through the filter, which can choose to (a) act and bypass working memory, (b) “ignore” information, or (c) pass the information on to working memory. The information passed onto working memory can be individual sensations or it can be patterns. Working memory processes these sensations and patterns to create situation awareness, which feeds into decision making, which results in action (or not) being taken on the world. In working memory there are also the processes of sensemaking (creating new patterns) and metacognition (thinking about thinking).
Press enter or click to view image in full size
a cartoon detailing the dual factor model and that automation does not change what the human cognition system does.
All processing in working memory requires what are called attention resources. Cognitive workload is defined as the number of resources required by working memory to complete a task in relation to the number of resources available. It should be noted that attention resources are theoretical constructs. As of yet, we cannot point to something physiological and say that is an attention resource. Despite this lack of knowledge as to what resources are physiologically, we know that they exist and that they are limited.
One of the best-known examples of research on the limited resources within Working Memory is George Miller’s Magical Number 7+/- 2. Essentially, Miller found that we can hold 7 chunks of information in working memory. A chunk is a pattern that has been passed on from the filter. As described in the first article, the filter groups sensations into patterns and uses selective attention to determine what patterns or sensations are sent on to working memory. This is done to ensure that the amount of information to be processed does not exceed the number of resources available. Because if the task(s) do require more resources than are available, then we are in a task overload situation and our performance degrades. When our performance degrades. So, the filter does what it can to keep us out of an overload situation.
Expertise, Resources, & Cognitive Workload
It is important to remember that the filter passes along patterns and these patterns are unique to each human, the amount of resources needed to complete a task is unique to each person. In other words the number of resources required to complete a task varies from person to person. Therefore the cognitive workload experienced in any given task varies from person to person.
One of the most studied phenomena in psychology and decision making is the differences between experts and novices on cognitive tasks. Through this research, scientists that the key distinction between experts and novices is the patterns in long term memory . This research has shown that experts’ patterns typically are more complex than those of novices (Grier, 2015). That is experts’ patterns contain more information than novices’ patterns. This means that in experts the filter passes on more information or at least the information is organized in a way that requires less resources to obtain situation awareness, which is a key input to the decision making process.
As described in the second article in this series, situation awareness is most commonly defined as “the perception of environmental elements and events with respect to time or space, the comprehension of their meaning, and the projection of their future status” (Endsley, 1988). More succinctly there are three levels of Situation Awareness: (1) perception, (2) comprehension, and (3) projection. The more situation awareness a person has, the better quality of his/her decision making.
As experts have more complex patterns than novices, they need to spend less resources to develop situation awareness. So experts experience less workload. These more complex patterns typically result in better performance with less workload for experts. That is the expert does not need to use resources to create meaning and projection as the filter has recognized the pattern and passed it on as 1 chunk to Working Memory. Malcolm Gladwell described in “Blink: The Power of Thinking Without Thinking,” they may instantaneously and unconsciously make a decision.
However, when this occurs experts rarely can describe why they came to that decision. And in fact, asking an expert to describe how they know something can lead to worse performance as they try to reconstruct the patterns in their long term memory and begin to question their decision making ability. Novices are far more capable of explaining why or how they do something than doing it. Thus supporting the adage, “those who can — do; those who cannot — teach.”
Another disadvantage of the expert is that when the pattern is passed on, it may pass along information that is not there. I am certain that everyone has written text and not realized there was a typo. This is an example of the filter passing along a pattern and not what was actually sensed. It is also how magicians do their illusions. They take advantage of the universal patterns so that we sense what they want us to sense and not what is happening.
To be clear, the cognitive workload does not correlate to the demands of the task. The same task can lead to different levels of cognitive workload depending on the people who are performing the task and their expertise. Physiological factors such as intoxication, illness/injury, hunger, and fatigue can impact the workload experienced. All of these and other non-physiological factors can cause us to experience stress, which can also impact the number of resources available.
Cognitive Workload, Stress, & Performance
Recall that the definition of workload is the number of resources required by working memory to complete a task in relation to the number of resources available. Resources are physiological; so if we are intoxicated, ill, injured, hungry, or tired, we will have fewer resources available. So even if a task requires the same number of resources on Monday and Tuesday, if on Tuesday we are tired/ill/hungry, we will experience higher workload due to fewer resources being available.
In addition, the number of resources available can change based on the experience of stress. We have heard the stories of people doing extraordinary things in moments of extreme stress. This is because in those instances additional resources (attention and physical) are made available for the fight or flight response. However, these additional attentional resources are only available for short periods of time. After which the number of resources available drops precipitously. The precipitous drop allows our bodies a chance to recharge the pool of resources available. It should be noted this recharge is necessary. If we do not recharge after extreme stress or we experience stress for an extended period of time, there will be permanent changes to the structure of the brain.
Get Rebecca Grier’s stories in your inbox
Join Medium for free to get updates from this writer.

Subscribe
With the exception of the extreme situations, it is well documented that performance does not improve as stress increases. In 1908, the Yerkes-Dodson law established that there is an optimal level of stress where our performance increases. Part of this is due to the number of resources available, but part of it is due to task unrelated thoughts.
If the number of resources required by a task is far below the number of resources available, attention resources may be diverted away from the task to the base motivations associated with the 3 S’s (i.e., sleep, sustenance, and love). That is our mind wanders to one of these topics instead of focusing on the task at hand.
Press enter or click to view image in full size
If the number of resources needed exceeds resources available, we are in an overload situation. If the number of resources needed are fewer than available, resources are diverted to thoughts of fatigue, food, & fornication. This leaves a very small space where the resources required of a task results in optimal task performance
Performance degrades when there are too many and too few resources required by a task.
When we experience these low demand situations and our thoughts start to wander, one of two things can happen: vigilance decrement or complacency. The vigilance decrement occurs with high stress tasks and complacency occurs with low stress tasks.
The vigilance decrement is one of the most robust, but seemingly paradoxical findings in human factors. It was first studied in WII; when RADAR was invented a new position in aircraft was created where operators would monitor the RADAR displays for a clear signal that there was a German U-boat in the waters. They would then alert other entities, who would attack the U-boat.
It seems like a simple task; look at this display for a clear blip. In fact, detection was near 1005 during the first 15 min of watch. However, after 15min of watch, the chance of detection decreased precipitously. Furthermore, the operators would return to base as tired as the pilots.
To the casual observer it looks like the person is doing very little. However, 50 years of research has shown that the person is expending a lot of attention resources on preventing their mind from wandering or staying awake, because they understand the risks of not detecting every signal. So they are expending a great deal of resources to keep the task unrelated thoughts out of their working memory. This high level of resource usage leads to high cognitive workload. The vigilance decrement is the reason life guards and transportation security guards switch locations every 15min.
Press enter or click to view image in full size
When too many resources are required for a task, performance degrades because of cognitive overload. When a person is experiencing low stress in a task, performance degrades because of complacency. When there is high stress, then performance degrades due to the vigilance decrement (low demand task) or cognitive tunnelling. In extreme stress, we have additional resources for the fight or flight response that can lead to extraordinary performance, but at a cost.
Stress and resources required interact to impact performance.
Conversely, complacency is the failure to adequately monitor a situation (i.e., maintain vigilance) due to self-satisfaction with performance. In other words, if we believe that the task does not demand all of our attention, then we will allow unrelated thoughts to use resources in our working memory. Complacency has resulted in numerous accidents during “routine” medical transport calls, long duration space flight, war, among other situations. Though it is instinctual to think of complacency as a human failing it is indeed a normal and adaptive behaviour to a situation in which fewer resources are available. The filter is “aware” that fewer resources are available, so it sends fewer things on for processing. Complacency also commonly happens when a task has become routine.
Complacency occurs in low stress tasks with moderate and low resource requirements. The vigilance decrement occurs in high stress tasks with low demands. Cognitive tunnelling is a phenomenon that occurs in high stress tasks with moderate demands. First described in combat pilots, cognitive tunnelling is when an individual has trouble making more strategic decisions. That is they are very much focused on the here and now and not on the wider context. It seems that stress reduces how much information working memory can process. Examples of cognitive tunnelling exist outside of the military domain. For example, medical doctors have been documented to make poor decisions after being awake for numerous hours. It has also been seen in daily life, when people are exposed to longer term stressors such as poverty.
Thus stress and resources required have an interactive effect on an individuals performance. There is an optimal level of stress and resource requirements where an individual will have the highest performance. In future articles, I will return to this concept and describe how leadership and other organizational factors can impact individual performance.
Multiple Types of Resources
Thus far, I have described resources as if they are one type. That isn’t quite accurate. Chris Wickens posited in 1984 that there are multiple pools of resources and all evidence supports this assertion. Each pool of resources is available for different types of information at different stages of processing. The three stages of processing are (1) perception, (2) analysis, and (3) action. Information can come in via different sensory systems, which is one dimension of type. A second dimension of type is whether it is linguistic or graphical/tonal. Each combination of information type and stage of processing has a dedicated pool of finite resources.
So one can be in an overload situation and still have available resources. Those resources are just in another pool. Multitasking is completely possible when using multiple pools of resources. There are limits though. Each of the three stages of processing have a finite limit that cannot be exceeded and each dimension of type of information have a finite number of resources. So, we are able to do more multi-tasking when the tasks use very different resources than when there is overlap in the tasking.
Press enter or click to view image in full size

The careful reader will notice that the 3 stages of processing do not align perfectly with the stages of processing in working memory. Perceptual resources are dedicated to attaining the first level of situation awareness, perception. Action resources are dedicated to taking action. Analysis resources for everything else that occurs in working memory. This includes attaining the second and third levels of situation awareness (i.e., comprehension & projection), decision making, sensemaking, and metacognition. Thus the patterns that are used by the filter are even more critical to reducing workload. As the analysis resources are used for most of working memory.
Summary
In summary, all the cognition that occurs in working memory requires attention resources. Cognitive workload is the number of attention resources required for a task compared to the number of attention resources available. The number of attention resources available can change based on our health and our experience of stress. When we are doing a task that does not have a lot of stimulation, our working memory will allow our mind to wander to our base motivations. If the task is important, then we will expend more resources to prevent mind wandering. Thus tasks that appear easy can be just as challenging as tasks that appear overwhelming in terms of information to be processed. Furthermore, there are multiple pools of resources. When tasks are spread across these pools, we can do more than when relying on a single pool. So when adding automation, we must consider how it changes the cognitive processes. This is best done through a task analysis and function allocation.
The next article will dive deeper into how to utilize this knowledge of the dual system model, resources, workload, & stress in the design of systems. This will talk in more detail about task analysis and function allocation. Future articles will also discuss how the user interface helps with creation of patterns known as mental models and how that impacts trust with automation, which is critical to successful human-system integration. Another topic for future articles in about how leadership and teammates can aid each other in staying in the zone of optimal performance.

- **Workload isn’t absolute.** The same task feels different depending on expertise, stress, and physical/mental state.  
- **Experts vs novices:** Experts use patterns in long-term memory to reduce cognitive load — but they can’t always explain their decisions.  
- **Stress isn’t all bad:** Some stress gives a temporary boost in attention/resources, but too much kills performance.  
- **The sweet spot:** Peak performance happens in a balance — not too few resources (complacency), not too many (overload).  
- **Multiple pools of attention:** We can multitask more effectively when tasks draw from different cognitive resources.  

For designers and product teams, the takeaway is clear: **our interfaces, workflows, and automation shouldn’t just look simple — they should actively manage users’ cognitive load.**

However, these additional attentional resources are only available for short periods of time. After which the number of resources available drops precipitously. The precipitous drop allows our bodies a chance to recharge the pool of resources available. It should be noted this recharge is necessary. If we do not recharge after extreme stress or we experience stress for an extended period of time, there will be permanent changes to the structure of the brain.

Join Medium for free to get updates from this writer.

Subscribe
With the exception of the extreme situations, it is well documented that performance does not improve as stress increases. In 1908, the Yerkes-Dodson law established that there is an optimal level of stress where our performance increases. Part of this is due to the number of resources available, but part of it is due to task unrelated thoughts.
If the number of resources required by a task is far below the number of resources available, attention resources may be diverted away from the task to the base motivations associated with the 3 S’s (i.e., sleep, sustenance, and love). That is our mind wanders to one of these topics instead of focusing on the task at hand.
Press enter or click to view image in full size
If the number of resources needed exceeds resources available, we are in an overload situation. If the number of resources needed are fewer than available, resources are diverted to thoughts of fatigue, food, & fornication. This leaves a very small space where the resources required of a task results in optimal task performance
Performance degrades when there are too many and too few resources required by a task.
When we experience these low demand situations and our thoughts start to wander, one of two things can happen: vigilance decrement or complacency. The vigilance decrement occurs with high stress tasks and complacency occurs with low stress tasks.
The vigilance decrement is one of the most robust, but seemingly paradoxical findings in human factors. It was first studied in WII; when RADAR was invented a new position in aircraft was created where operators would monitor the RADAR displays for a clear signal that there was a German U-boat in the waters. They would then alert other entities, who would attack the U-boat.
It seems like a simple task; look at this display for a clear blip. In fact, detection was near 1005 during the first 15 min of watch. However, after 15min of watch, the chance of detection decreased precipitously. Furthermore, the operators would return to base as tired as the pilots.
To the casual observer it looks like the person is doing very little. However, 50 years of research has shown that the person is expending a lot of attention resources on preventing their mind from wandering or staying awake, because they understand the risks of not detecting every signal. So they are expending a great deal of resources to keep the task unrelated thoughts out of their working memory. This high level of resource usage leads to high cognitive workload. The vigilance decrement is the reason life guards and transportation security guards switch locations every 15min.
Press enter or click to view image in full size
When too many resources are required for a task, performance degrades because of cognitive overload. When a person is experiencing low stress in a task, performance degrades because of complacency. When there is high stress, then performance degrades due to the vigilance decrement (low demand task) or cognitive tunnelling. In extreme stress, we have additional resources for the fight or flight response that can lead to extraordinary performance, but at a cost.
Stress and resources required interact to impact performance.
Conversely, complacency is the failure to adequately monitor a situation (i.e., maintain vigilance) due to self-satisfaction with performance. In other words, if we believe that the task does not demand all of our attention, then we will allow unrelated thoughts to use resources in our working memory. Complacency has resulted in numerous accidents during “routine” medical transport calls, long duration space flight, war, among other situations. Though it is instinctual to think of complacency as a human failing it is indeed a normal and adaptive behaviour to a situation in which fewer resources are available. The filter is “aware” that fewer resources are available, so it sends fewer things on for processing. Complacency also commonly happens when a task has become routine.
Complacency occurs in low stress tasks with moderate and low resource requirements. The vigilance decrement occurs in high stress tasks with low demands. Cognitive tunnelling is a phenomenon that occurs in high stress tasks with moderate demands. First described in combat pilots, cognitive tunnelling is when an individual has trouble making more strategic decisions. That is they are very much focused on the here and now and not on the wider context. It seems that stress reduces how much information working memory can process. Examples of cognitive tunnelling exist outside of the military domain. For example, medical doctors have been documented to make poor decisions after being awake for numerous hours. It has also been seen in daily life, when people are exposed to longer term stressors such as poverty.
Thus stress and resources required have an interactive effect on an individuals performance. There is an optimal level of stress and resource requirements where an individual will have the highest performance. In future articles, I will return to this concept and describe how leadership and other organizational factors can impact individual performance.
Multiple Types of Resources
Thus far, I have described resources as if they are one type. That isn’t quite accurate. Chris Wickens posited in 1984 that there are multiple pools of resources and all evidence supports this assertion. Each pool of resources is available for different types of information at different stages of processing. The three stages of processing are (1) perception, (2) analysis, and (3) action. Information can come in via different sensory systems, which is one dimension of type. A second dimension of type is whether it is linguistic or graphical/tonal. Each combination of information type and stage of processing has a dedicated pool of finite resources.
So one can be in an overload situation and still have available resources. Those resources are just in another pool. Multitasking is completely possible when using multiple pools of resources. There are limits though. Each of the three stages of processing have a finite limit that cannot be exceeded and each dimension of type of information have a finite number of resources. So, we are able to do more multi-tasking when the tasks use very different resources than when there is overlap in the tasking.
Press enter or click to view image in full size

The careful reader will notice that the 3 stages of processing do not align perfectly with the stages of processing in working memory. Perceptual resources are dedicated to attaining the first level of situation awareness, perception. Action resources are dedicated to taking action. Analysis resources for everything else that occurs in working memory. This includes attaining the second and third levels of situation awareness (i.e., comprehension & projection), decision making, sensemaking, and metacognition. Thus the patterns that are used by the filter are even more critical to reducing workload. As the analysis resources are used for most of working memory.
Summary
In summary, all the cognition that occurs in working memory requires attention resources. Cognitive workload is the number of attention resources required for a task compared to the number of attention resources available. The number of attention resources available can change based on our health and our experience of stress. When we are doing a task that does not have a lot of stimulation, our working memory will allow our mind to wander to our base motivations. If the task is important, then we will expend more resources to prevent mind wandering. Thus tasks that appear easy can be just as challenging as tasks that appear overwhelming in terms of information to be processed. Furthermore, there are multiple pools of resources. When tasks are spread across these pools, we can do more than when relying on a single pool. So when adding automation, we must consider how it changes the cognitive processes. This is best done through a task analysis and function allocation.
The next article will dive deeper into how to utilize this knowledge of the dual system model, resources, workload, & stress in the design of systems. This will talk in more detail about task analysis and function allocation. Future articles will also discuss how the user interface helps with creation of patterns known as mental models and how that impacts trust with automation, which is critical to successful human-system integration. Another topic for future articles in about how leadership and teammates can aid each other in staying in the zone of optimal performance.

⚡ **We design for flow states. But do we even understand what breaks them?**

Rebecca Grier’s *Designing Technology with the Human Mind in Mind* series (Part IV) is one of those rare reminders that UX is first and foremost *a cognitive science*.  
This installment dives into **workload, stress, and total system performance** — the invisible architecture shaping how people perceive, decide, and act.

She revisits what the field once built upon —  
- **Miller’s 7±2 rule** on memory limits  
- **Yerkes-Dodson Law (1908)** on optimal stress and performance  
- **Endsley’s Situation Awareness model (1988)** — perception → comprehension → projection  
- **Wickens’ Multiple Resource Theory (1984)** — why true multitasking is an illusion  

Key takeaways:  
🧠 Expertise = compressed pattern recognition that frees up cognitive resources.  
⚙️ Stress narrows perception — performance only peaks within a narrow “optimal load.”  
💡 Design’s true goal isn’t just clarity; it’s *resource allocation* within human attention.

> “Automation doesn’t change what the human cognitive system does — it changes how it struggles.”

In an era obsessed with AI and automation, this is a grounding reminder: **great UX design isn’t decoration, it’s cognitive empathy**.  
We’ve been here before — aviation, medicine, defense — and their lessons about human limits are as urgent now as ever.

Highly recommend reading the full series for anyone building complex systems, fintech tools, or AI-powered experiences.

Why We Rejected the Super App Model for a Vertical Insurance Platform Redesign: Phase 1
Focus: Setting the stage, defining the problem, and the first critical decision (information architecture).
The Initial Mandate: Navigating the Strategic Crossroads:
Our project's first strategic win was validating the foundational information architecture (IA) through an immediate, targeted usability test. By decoupling architectural decisions from the aesthetic redesign, we proved that the Top-Bar navigation approach was the most efficient structure for managing a complex, multi-product ecosystem - directly supporting the corporate mandate to increase engagement and retention.
When tackling the redesign of a major mobile financial application, the first hurdle isn't visual - it's strategic. The architectural foundation determines every subsequent decision: navigation, content allocation, and long-term scalability.
Our journey began nine months ago with a clear goal - to transform a complex, legacy insurance app into a cohesive, engagement-driven platform. This is the story of how a single, high-stakes usability test validated our most crucial early decision.
I. The Challenge: A Burden of Complexity in a Reactive Sector
Strategic Shift: From Mass to PersonalizedBefore the redesign, the application reflected the typical struggles of mature financial products: high complexity and user friction. These were compounded by the inherently reactive nature of insurance - customers usually engage only after an adverse event (an accident, a claim, a health issue).
Prior to redesign - Allianz'ım AppOver time, the user experience had evolved organically, leading to fragmented information, inconsistent flows, and an outdated visual system. Key pain points were clear:
1. High Cognitive Load
Customers with multiple policies (Health, BES, Vehicle) found it difficult to locate information or complete routine tasks - especially in urgent situations. The use of a horizontal carousel to display policies forced users to swipe repeatedly to find details (e.g., from Health to Vehicle coverage). This interaction model increased cognitive load and wasted precious time, particularly in moments of crisis.
2. Limited Guidance & Cross-Sell
The application functioned mainly as a policy repository, not a financial guidance tool. The mid-section's "promiscuous" information architecture gave equal weight to self-service actions and external promotions, creating sensory overload. This lack of hierarchy obscured cross-sell opportunities and prevented the app from becoming an active engagement channel.
3. Architectural Failure & Dated UI
The Bottom Navigation Bar had reached its scalability limits, evidenced by the existence of a vague "Other" tab - an architectural catch-all for critical but non-core products. Combined with a dated UI, the experience failed to convey the professionalism and trustworthiness expected from a leading financial brand.
The Initial Mandate: Executing the Transformation
The strategic objective was to establish a modern, engagement-driven platform that would serve as the primary digital relationship channel between Allianz and its customers.
This vision aligned with a bold corporate mandate:
Transition from a traditional, agency-based model to a leading mobile insurance provider in Turkey within two years - achieving 50–60% mobile usage.
To reach this target, the platform needed to evolve through two key phases:
Phase 1: Operational Efficiency - Migrate agency functions to self-service (this phase was nearly complete).
Phase 2: Engagement & Retention - Improve usability, NPS, and satisfaction to drive retention and cross-sell.

The core transformation was therefore about shifting from documentation to activation and guidance - moving the app from a "Past/Today" model to a Future State that delivers personalized, value-driven solutions across both Lines of Business (LoB) and digital touchpoints.
Team & Timeline
The project officially launched in January 2025 as a collaboration between Ting (UX Design Partner), Product Management, and Development.
Operating in parallel tracks, our initial goal was to establish a functional navigation framework - allowing content strategy and component design to progress simultaneously.

---

II. Decisive Action: Choosing the Navigation Pattern
First Sketches of the Potential Navigation ApproachesBefore designing a single component, we faced a critical decision: selecting the structure that would govern the app's deep hierarchy - its Information Architecture.
The conceptual design phase narrowed the options to two models:
HUB (Super App Card Model)
Top Navigation Bar (Top-Bar)

The Great Debate: Top-Bar vs. Super App Card
Pros & Cons of Both ApproachesThe Rationale for NavBar (The Top-Bar)
We leaned toward the NavBar (Top-Bar) approach for strategic reasons:
Professional Identity & Urgency
The reactive nature of insurance demands quick, high-stakes actions - reporting an accident, checking coverage, initiating claims. The Top-Bar structure aligns with this urgency, presenting a professional, utilitarian identity rather than the promotional aesthetic of a HUB model.
Content Allocation & Clarity
The Top-Bar system, paired with contextual sub-filters, solved the "acuity challenge." Each product line received the space it needed without cluttering the dashboard. This design reserved the majority of screen real estate for dynamic, personalized content, essential to achieving our engagement goals.
Discoverability as a Growth Lever
Consolidating navigation controls at the top freed the lower two-thirds of the screen for Dynamic Content - allowing us to surface personalized insights, value-driven offers, and contextual cross-sell opportunities. The navigation choice thus became a commercial growth mechanism, not just a usability improvement.

First Deployment: The Test Track
NavBar (Top-Bar) Version for the Usability TestTo confirm our strategic choice - and minimize risk - we made a crucial pragmatic decision: we wouldn't wait for the new UI.
Instead, we:
Created a basic prototype using the Top-Bar structure.
Mapped this new navigation system onto existing live screens.
Conducted immediate usability testing with current users.

The objective was straightforward: could users easily find what they needed when navigation elements moved from the bottom to the top?
This test allowed us to validate user mental models and information architecture performance before committing to months of full development. It was a deliberate exercise in decoupling structural validation from visual design - a principle that would guide the rest of the project.
The success of this approach established the tone for a data-driven, agile process, setting the stage for the decisive usability insights that followed.
What's Next
In Phase 2, we'll share the usability test findings and how these insights shaped our content strategy and component architecture for the next iteration.

---

It was about redefining the digital relationship model in a reactive sector - turning structural design into a strategic lever for engagement, clarity, and long-term retention.

**Title:** Why Neural Efficiency Should Be a Design Metric in Regulated Industries  

---

When you design in a regulated industry — like insurance or finance — complexity isn’t an exception, it’s the baseline. Every interface you build carries layers of compliance, legal wording, and policy logic. Every user flow has to make sense not only to a customer but also to auditors, regulators, and internal reviewers.  

Over time, you realize: the challenge isn’t about aesthetics, or even usability in the narrow sense. It’s about **reducing cognitive friction** in systems where every action must be both *understandable* and *defensible*.  

That’s where the concept of **neural efficiency** becomes deeply relevant.  

---

### What Neural Efficiency Really Means  

In neuroscience, *neural efficiency* refers to how experts use fewer cognitive resources to perform the same tasks as novices. Their brains activate more precisely, less wastefully. In other words — they think *smarter*, not *harder*.  

In product design, that same principle can be translated into **clarity of decision pathways**. How many steps, how many terms, how many interpretations does a user — or an employee — have to process before acting confidently and correctly?  

The less cognitive energy it takes to make the right move, the more *neural-efficient* your product is.  

---

### Why It Matters in Regulated Systems  

Regulated industries depend on **trust**, **clarity**, and **compliance** — three pillars that often get in each other’s way.  

- **Trust** collapses when users feel overwhelmed by unclear information.  
- **Clarity** suffers when compliance requirements overtake communication.  
- **Compliance** breaks when clarity and trust are lost.  

Neural efficiency acts as a bridge between these forces. It’s not about oversimplifying, but about structuring complexity so people can process it efficiently.  

Executives already talk about *risk reduction* and *compliance assurance*. Neural efficiency adds a cognitive layer to those metrics: how well can users — internal or external — navigate critical decisions *without hesitation or confusion*?  

If an interface causes users to pause, re-read, or guess, that’s not just bad UX. It’s **operational risk** disguised as design debt.  

---

### Neural Efficiency as a Strategic Design Metric  

In fast-moving industries, we measure velocity, engagement, retention — but not *neural load*. Yet it’s neural load that determines how resilient and scalable a product becomes.  

Imagine tracking **neural efficiency** alongside NPS or conversion rates:  
- How quickly do new users reach confident understanding?  
- How consistent are decisions across different user types?  
- How much mental effort is required to stay compliant?  

Designers can quantify this with techniques borrowed from cognitive science and usability testing — eye-tracking, error rates, decision time, even subjective cognitive load assessments.  

These insights can feed directly into **liability management**: the less cognitive confusion, the fewer missteps, complaints, and compliance escalations.  

---

### The Bigger Shift  

Designing for neural efficiency means designing for *shared mental models*.  

When customers, agents, and regulators all interpret the same information consistently, the system runs smoother. Documentation becomes shorter. Onboarding becomes cheaper. Compliance becomes natural — not forced.  

In regulated environments, this isn’t an aesthetic pursuit. It’s **strategic infrastructure** for reducing uncertainty and friction at scale.  

---

### Final Thought  

In industries where precision and perception define success, **neural efficiency isn’t luxury — it’s liability management**.  

It’s the invisible architecture that makes trust scalable, compliance humane, and clarity profitable.

# Why Neural Efficiency Should Be a Design Metric in Regulated Industries

When I design products for insurance and finance, I don’t just think about screens — I think about decisions. People who use our products are often making important, stressful choices: buying coverage, confirming identity, authorizing payments, or filing a claim. In those moments, the product is not merely an interface; it’s part of the decision-maker’s brain.

That’s why I believe **neural efficiency** — the degree to which a user completes tasks while using minimal cognitive resources — should be an explicit design metric in regulated industries. Measured and managed properly, neural efficiency aligns with three things executives care about: **trust**, **clarity**, and **compliance**. More importantly, it reduces operational and regulatory risk by keeping users in the cognitive zone where they can make correct decisions quickly and reliably.

Below I explain the concept, show why it matters specifically for insurance and finance, offer practical ways to measure it (without needing a brain scanner), and give a playbook for embedding it into product development and governance.

---

## What is neural efficiency — in plain terms?

In cognitive neuroscience, *neural efficiency* describes a pattern where experts perform tasks equally well (or better) than novices while showing lower levels of neural activation. In short: they **use less brain energy** to reach the same result. This has been observed across domains — intelligence studies, sports performance, even complex problem-solving tasks.

Translated to product design: a neurally efficient interface helps users get to correct decisions with **less mental effort**, less time, and fewer errors. The goal isn’t to “simplify everything” — it’s to design so the right cognitive resources are available at the right time.

Key cognitive ideas that shape this definition:

- **Working memory is limited.** We can only hold a few “chunks” in working memory at a time (think Miller’s 7±2). Interfaces that force users to hold many items mentally increase error and slow decisions.  
- **Stress and workload interact.** The Yerkes–Dodson law shows there’s an optimal level of arousal for performance — too little and people are disengaged; too much and they tunnel. Regulated-product moments often sit near the “too much” side.  
- **Multiple resource pools.** Not all mental work is the same: perception, analysis, and action draw on different cognitive pools (Wickens’ theory). Good design leverages multiple channels rather than saturating one.

---

## Why regulated industries need neural efficiency more than others

1. **High-stakes decisions under constraints.** A customer buying a disability rider, or an agent approving a large claim, is weighing financial, legal, and personal consequences. Cognitive overload here creates mistakes that cascade into liability or regulatory scrutiny.

2. **Regulatory clarity depends on comprehension.** Compliance isn’t only about showing boxes checked in an audit trail; it’s about whether a customer *understood* what they agreed to. Cognitive overload increases the risk of misinformed consent — and fines.

3. **Trust is fragile and micro-interaction-driven.** In sectors where trust is the product, every friction point (a confusing dropdown, unclear confirmation language, or a slow step during a claim) is a trust tax. Neurally efficient flows reduce the moments that erode confidence.

4. **Cost of failure is high.** Unlike consumer apps where a poor experience means churn, in finance/insurance failures can mean fraud, compliance breaches, litigation, refunds, or brand damage. Decreasing cognitive error is risk mitigation.

---

## How neural efficiency maps to executive outcomes

Executives talk in terms of revenue, cost, and risk. Neural efficiency translates directly:

- **Risk reduction:** fewer decision errors → fewer disputes, fewer regulatory escalations, fewer compensations.  
- **Frictionless compliance:** clearer choices and fewer ambiguous states lead to higher rates of valid consent and audit-ready records.  
- **Operational efficiency:** simpler decision flows reduce CS calls, rework, and manual interventions.  
- **Conversion and retention:** when the brain spends less energy and gets predictable outcomes, trust and loyalty increase.

Framing neural efficiency as a risk/return lever — not just “UX niceness” — is how you get executive and compliance buy-in.

---

## Practical metrics (what to measure — without neurotech)

Full neuroimaging is fascinating for research labs, but product teams need practical proxies. Below are reliable, measurable signals that correlate with cognitive load and decision quality:

### Behavioral proxies (low friction)
- **Task completion time** — longer times often indicate cognitive load or friction.  
- **Error and reversal rates** — number of corrected inputs, abandoned steps, or help requests.  
- **Drop-off at decision points** — where users hesitate or abandon during consent/checkout/claim steps.  
- **Help calls & escalation volume** — spikes after a rollout can indicate increased mental effort.  
- **Rework / manual override rate** — operations needing human fix-ups shows automated processes confused users.

### UX signals (more diagnostic)
- **Click/interaction heatmaps** — show where users hesitate or backtrack.  
- **Time-on-screen for critical pages** — long dwell with no progress suggests comprehension issues.  
- **Micro-surveys (single-item cognitive load)** — e.g., “How easy was it to complete this task?” or NASA-TLX light variant.  
- **Pupilometry & eye-tracking (when available in tests)** — physiological signs of load; useful in lab studies.  
- **A/B experiments with simplified variants** — measure downstream outcomes (fraud flags, claims accuracy).

### Business & compliance signals
- **Regulatory inquiry frequency** — increased support for certain flows may lead to more regulators’ attention.  
- **Customer dispute & refund rates** — can be traced to misunderstanding in consent or claims.  
- **Time to resolution for investigations** — longer times often involve misread information streams.

---

## How to build neural efficiency into delivery (playbook)

### 1) Make it a metric in discovery
Start with a cognitive problem statement in discovery — not just “users can’t find X,” but “users expend X mental steps to decide Y.” Use a simple cognitive task map to show steps, memory load, and stress points.

### 2) Use layered prototyping with cognitive validation
- **Low-fi cognitive walkthroughs** — ask participants to “think aloud” focusing on what they’re holding in mind.  
- **High-fi lab tests** — use eye-tracking or micro-surveys to validate trade-offs for critical flows (claims, onboarding, KYC).  
- **In-market small rollouts** — test simplified variants and measure the behavioral proxies above.

### 3) Design patterns that increase neural efficiency
- **Recognition over recall.** Replace input-heavy forms with selectable options, defaults, and smart prefill.  
- **Progressive disclosure.** Only surface the next decision when it matters.  
- **Chunking and semantic grouping.** Group related information into a single cognitive chunk.  
- **Contextual affordances.** Use microcopy and inline examples that map the concept to users’ lives (reduces mental model construction).  
- **Decision scaffolding.** Provide decision summaries and “what happens next” to reduce projection load.

### 4) Embed into governance & compliance reviews
Make neural efficiency part of your compliance sign-off. Instead of a binary legal checklist, include a lightweight cognitive audit: “can an average user explain their choice after completing this flow?” Require a test metric (e.g., 80% comprehension in a short survey) for signoff.

### 5) Train product & ops teams
Operational teams (claims handlers, agents) should understand cognitive load, so they can spot systemic issues early. Use simple playbooks: “If users call more than X times in week Y, suspect cognitive overload and run a quick task analysis.”

---

## A short hypothetical: claims submission flow

Imagine a long-form claims flow with 15 fields, conditional sections, technical jargon, and few inline examples. After launch, fraud checks and manual reviews spike by 30%, and customer complaints about “unclear questions” double.

A neural-efficiency approach would:

1. Map cognitive steps and identify where users must hold multiple facts.  
2. Convert repeated recall tasks to recognition (upload photos instead of manual descriptions; use auto-detected locations).  
3. Break the flow into progressive confirmation steps with clear “why we ask” microcopy.  
4. Pilot the simplified variant and measure error rate, time-to-complete, and manual-review rate.

Result: fewer errors, faster processing, lower manual review — i.e., lower operational cost and lower regulatory exposure.

---

## Caveats and governance issues

- **Neural efficiency is not manipulation.** The goal is to reduce unnecessary cognitive friction so decisions are clearer — not to nudge people into unfavorable outcomes. Ethics and consent are essential guardrails.  
- **Context matters.** Experts can handle denser information but may miss novel cues; novices need scaffolding. Segment and test.  
- **Measurement needs rigor.** Don’t confuse speed for quality. Pair behavioral metrics with comprehension checks and downstream outcomes.

---

## How to present this to executives

If you’re pitching this internally, lead with three things executives care about:

1. **Risk:** “We reduce dispute and regulatory risk by X% by improving decision comprehension.”  
2. **Cost:** “We cut manual review & CS costs by Y% by lowering error rates.”  
3. **Growth:** “Fewer friction points increase conversion and retention; simpler flows convert better during onboarding.”

Offer a small, time-boxed pilot (e.g., claims submission or onboarding) with clear KPIs: task completion, error rate, manual review reduction, and a comprehension micro-survey.

---

## Further reading (selected studies that define the idea)

- Neubauer, A. C., & Fink, A. (2009). *Intelligence and neural efficiency: Measures of brain activation vs. functional connectivity.* (Foundational work on expertise and efficiency.)  
- Poldrack, R. (2015). *Is “Efficiency” a Useful Concept in Cognitive Neuroscience?* (A constructive critique — useful to define limits of the term.)  
- Causse, M., et al. (2017). *Mental workload and neural efficiency quantified in the prefrontal cortex using fNIRS.* (Empirical link between workload and neural activation.)  
- Wickens, C. (1984). *Multiple Resource Theory.* (On how different types of cognitive resources are taxed.)  
- Endsley, M. (1988). *Situation Awareness Model.* (Perception → comprehension → projection; crucial for high-stakes flows.)

(Include links or attach bibliography for reviewers and compliance.)

---

## Closing

Design in regulated industries is not an aesthetic exercise. It’s a systems problem where human cognition sits at the center of risk, trust, and compliance. By reframing good UX as **neural efficiency** — and by making it measurable, testable, and governable — product teams can reduce operational costs, lower regulatory exposure, and build trust that scales.

**In regulated systems, neural efficiency isn’t luxury — it’s liability management.**

# Why Neural Efficiency Should Be a Design Metric in Regulated Industries

When I design products in insurance and finance, I don’t just think about screens — I think about decisions.  
Every interaction is a moment of judgment: confirming identity, buying coverage, or submitting a claim.  

In these moments, the product becomes part of the decision-maker’s brain.  
And that’s where **neural efficiency** enters the picture — not as a neuroscience buzzword, but as a practical design principle for systems where **clarity, trust, and compliance** define success.

---

## What Neural Efficiency Really Means

In cognitive science, *neural efficiency* describes how experts solve problems faster and more accurately than novices — while using **less mental energy**. Their brains literally “light up less” because they’ve organized the task efficiently.

In design terms, neural efficiency means helping users reach correct outcomes with minimal cognitive friction.

It’s not about dumbing down experiences.  
It’s about making the **right decisions easier to make** — by structuring information, timing, and feedback in a way that matches how the human brain naturally processes complexity.

When we ignore this, we don’t just frustrate users. We increase operational risk, slow down compliance, and multiply error loops across systems.

---

## Why Regulated Industries Need It Most

Neural efficiency matters in every digital product.  
But in **regulated industries** like banking and insurance, the stakes are higher — because mistakes have legal and financial consequences.

### 1. High-stakes decisions under stress  
Customers choosing coverage or submitting claims aren’t just “completing tasks.” They’re making irreversible decisions under uncertainty. Every unnecessary click or confusing phrase adds cognitive load that can lead to costly errors.

### 2. Compliance depends on comprehension  
Regulatory compliance isn’t achieved when checkboxes are ticked. It’s achieved when the customer **understands** what they’ve consented to. Cognitive overload undermines informed consent — and turns usability debt into regulatory risk.

### 3. Trust is a cognitive state  
In insurance, trust *is* the product. Every confusing step — unclear confirmation text, ambiguous feedback, or unexplained delay — erodes that trust. Neural efficiency builds the opposite: confidence, clarity, predictability.

### 4. Complexity multiplies downstream costs  
When flows are mentally demanding, users make errors. Errors lead to manual reviews, longer resolution times, and compliance escalations. Reducing cognitive friction reduces operational waste.

That’s why **neural efficiency isn’t just UX quality** — it’s a **risk control mechanism**.

---

## Translating to Executive Language

Executives don’t talk about “cognitive load.” They talk about **risk**, **cost**, and **growth**.  
The bridge is straightforward:

| Neural Efficiency | Executive Language |
|--------------------|-------------------|
| Reduces decision errors | Risk reduction |
| Improves understanding of consent | Compliance assurance |
| Cuts rework and CS calls | Operational efficiency |
| Increases trust and satisfaction | Retention & loyalty |

When a design team shows how simplifying decision paths reduces both user frustration *and* regulatory exposure, that’s when the conversation changes. Neural efficiency becomes a **governance tool**, not just a UX principle.

---

## Measuring Neural Efficiency Without a Brain Scanner

You don’t need fMRI to see cognitive load in action. It’s visible in the data — if you know where to look.

### Behavioral indicators
- Longer **completion times** for simple tasks  
- **Error reversals** (backtracking, corrections)  
- **Drop-offs** at decision-heavy screens  
- **Help desk spikes** post-launch  
- **Rework or manual overrides** in operations

### UX signals
- **Heatmaps** showing hesitation zones  
- **Eye-tracking dwell times** on dense copy  
- **Micro-surveys** (“This step was easy to complete” – 5-point scale)  
- **A/B test outcomes** showing efficiency vs. comprehension trade-offs

### Compliance signals
- **Informed-consent comprehension rates**  
- **Dispute and refund frequencies**  
- **Regulatory inquiry volume**  
- **Time to resolution** for claim or fraud disputes  

Together, these metrics tell you where the brain is struggling — and where design can intervene.

---

## Designing for Neural Efficiency

Here’s how to embed it directly into your design practice:

### 1. Start with a cognitive map  
Instead of only mapping user journeys, map **mental steps**: what users need to hold, compare, or infer at each point. The more items in working memory, the higher the risk of overload.

### 2. Shift from recall to recognition  
Use defaults, prefilled data, and contextual cues. Recognition reduces cognitive effort — the brain prefers seeing to remembering.

### 3. Apply progressive disclosure  
Show what’s relevant when it’s relevant. Don’t expose all conditions, explanations, or options at once. Information is easier to digest in sequence than in bulk.

### 4. Scaffolding decisions  
Give short “why we ask” notes beside critical fields. Users perform better when they understand purpose — it anchors comprehension.

### 5. Test comprehension, not just completion  
Completion rate shows usability. **Comprehension rate shows safety.** After a test task, ask users to explain what they agreed to — and act on what you learn.

---

## Building Governance Around It

To make neural efficiency part of the system, not just a design choice:

- Add a **Cognitive Load Review** to compliance sign-offs: “Can a typical customer accurately explain their decision afterward?”  
- Include **comprehension metrics** in success criteria — not just “fewer clicks” or “faster time.”  
- Train operations and compliance teams to recognize cognitive bottlenecks: a sudden rise in errors often means mental friction, not negligence.  

Once integrated, neural efficiency becomes part of **organizational hygiene**, much like accessibility or security.

---

## A Quick Example: Claims Submission Flow

A typical insurance claim form has 15+ fields, multiple conditional questions, and technical jargon.  
After rollout, call center volumes rise 25%, and claim-processing errors increase.

A neural-efficiency audit reveals that users must mentally track multiple pieces of information while switching between pages.

Simplifying the flow — auto-filling data, breaking it into smaller steps, adding “why we ask” text — reduces completion time by 30%, manual reviews by 40%, and complaint rates by half.

That’s not aesthetic improvement. That’s **risk mitigation through cognition**.

---

## Final Thought

Design in regulated industries isn’t decoration. It’s **decision infrastructure** — a shared cognitive layer between humans, systems, and laws.  

The more efficiently a product helps people think, the safer and more scalable it becomes.

So maybe it’s time to treat neural efficiency not as a “nice-to-have,” but as a **core design KPI** — measured, governed, and improved like any other form of system performance.

Because in regulated systems, **neural efficiency isn’t luxury — it’s liability management.**
